fitter_kind: str = 'proportional hazards fitter'

The repr (#614)

hf(x: NDArray | float, Z: NDArray | float, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

Hazard rate \(\phi(Z) h_0(x)\) at x for covariates Z; params as for Hf(), and on the log scale where \(h_0(x)\) is very small as Hf() is, with \(\log h_0 = \log f_0 - \log S_0\).

log_df(x: NDArray | float, Z: NDArray | float, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

The log density, log h - H, with log h taken as log phi + log h0 where h0 is very small (see above).

name_suffix: str = 'PH'

The end of the public name of a family’s fitter after its distribution’s, for a fitter without a name (WeibullAFT).

neg_ll(data: SurpyvalData, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

The negative log-likelihood of data at params (the distribution parameters followed by the covariate parameters), for every kind of censoring and truncation.

random(size: int, Z: ArrayLike, *params: float, random_state: Any = None) → tuple[NDArray, NDArray]

Draw size samples for each covariate row of Z.

Returns the draws and a 2-D array of the covariate row each was drawn at, row by row. random_state seeds the draw: None (the default) draws from numpy’s global generator, so np.random.seed reproduces it; an int or a numpy.random.Generator gives a stream of its own.

sf(x: NDArray | float, Z: NDArray | float, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

Survival function at x for covariates Z, \(R(x \mid Z) = e^{-H(x \mid Z)}\).

params are the distribution parameters followed by the covariate coefficients, in the order of a fitted model’s params. A fitted model’s own sf(x, Z) supplies them.

Accelerated Failure Time (AFT)

\[H(x \mid Z) = H_0\!\left(e^{\beta'Z} \cdot x\right)\]

Pre-built instances: ExponentialAFT, NormalAFT, WeibullAFT, GumbelAFT, LogisticAFT, LogNormalAFT, GammaAFT.

surpyval.univariate.regression.accelerated_failure_time.aft_fitter.AFT(distribution: Any) → AFTFitter

Create an Accelerated Failure Time fitter for the given distribution.

Uses exp(beta’Z) as the acceleration factor — the standard statistical parameterisation for AFT models.

Parameters:

distribution (ParametricFitter) – A surpyval parametric distribution (e.g. Weibull, LogNormal).

Returns:

A configured fitter with a .fit(x, Z, ...) method.

Return type:

AFTFitter

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import Weibull
>>> from surpyval import AFT
>>> np.random.seed(1)
>>> Z = np.random.binomial(1, 0.5, 100).reshape(-1, 1)
>>> x = Weibull.random(100, 10, 2) * np.exp(-0.5 * Z[:, 0])
>>> model = AFT(Weibull).fit(x, Z=Z)
>>> model.params.round(3)
array([9.629, 1.751, 0.473])
class surpyval.univariate.regression.accelerated_failure_time.aft_fitter.AFTFitter(distribution: Any)

Bases: HazardIdentitiesMixin, AFTTVCFitMixin, LogLinearRegressionFitter

Accelerated Failure Time fitter using \(e^{\beta' Z}\) as the acceleration factor. The covariates rescale time:

\[H(x \mid Z) = H_0\left(e^{\beta' Z} x\right), \qquad R(x \mid Z) = R_0\left(e^{\beta' Z} x\right).\]

A positive beta coefficient means higher covariate values accelerate failure (shorter life), consistent with the PH sign convention. (Many texts write the AFT model with \(e^{-\beta' Z}\), so their coefficients have the opposite sign.)

Use the pre-built instances (WeibullAFT, LogNormalAFT, …) or the AFT factory.

Hf(x: NDArray | float, Z: NDArray | float, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

Cumulative hazard \(H_0(e^{\beta' Z} x)\) at x for covariates Z; params are the distribution parameters followed by the covariate coefficients.

df(x: NDArray | float, Z: NDArray | float, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

Density at x for covariates Z, \(f(x \mid Z) = h(x \mid Z) e^{-H(x \mid Z)}\). params as for sf().

Far in the upper tail, where \(H\) is so large that \(e^{-H}\) underflows to 0, the density is 0, also where the hazard itself has overflowed to inf (a large Weibull shape, or a covariate far from 0): it is not inf * 0 (#714).

ff(x: NDArray | float, Z: NDArray | float, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

Failure (CDF) function at x for covariates Z, \(F(x \mid Z) = 1 - e^{-H(x \mid Z)}\). params as for sf().

fit(x: ArrayLike, Z: ArrayLike, c: ArrayLike | None = None, n: ArrayLike | None = None, t: ArrayLike | None = None, init: ArrayLike | None = None, fixed: dict[str, float] | None = None, center: bool = False, tl: ArrayLike | None = None, tr: ArrayLike | None = None, w: ArrayLike | float | None = None, *, unit=None) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit the accelerated failure time model by maximum likelihood.

Parameters:

  • x (array_like) – The observed event times.

  • Z (array_like) – The covariate matrix, one row per observation (a 1-D array is read as a single covariate). Rows with a missing or infinite covariate are dropped, with a warning.

  • c (array_like, optional) – The censoring indicators (0 observed, 1 right, -1 left, 2 interval). Defaults to all observed.

  • n (array_like, optional) – The count of observations at each time. Defaults to 1.

  • t (array_like, optional) – Truncation bounds: an (N, 2) array of the left and right truncation times of each observation.

  • tl (array_like or float, optional) – The left / right truncation times of each observation (or one for every observation), the columns of t, which they replace (#662).

  • tr (array_like or float, optional) – The left / right truncation times of each observation (or one for every observation), the columns of t, which they replace (#662).

  • init (array_like, optional) – Initial parameter values: the distribution parameters followed by the covariate coefficients.

  • fixed (dict, optional) – Parameters to hold fixed, by name (a distribution parameter such as "beta", or a coefficient: its covariate’s column name, else "coef_0", …).

  • center (bool, optional) – False (the default) reports the baseline at Z = 0. True reports the baseline at the covariate means (stored as model.center) instead: the fit runs on Z - center, and init and fixed are read there too. Use it for covariates far from 0 (a year, a date), where the baseline at Z = 0 cannot be represented or fitted, which the default fit refuses with a ValueError saying so.

  • w (array_like or float, optional) – Sampling, propensity or censoring weights, one positive number per row (beside its count n). The fit maximises the weighted (pseudo) likelihood and covariance(), behind every Wald bound, is the robust (sandwich) covariance, as R’s survreg(..., weights = w, robust = TRUE); the likelihood-ratio and bootstrap bounds and the information criteria refuse (see Weighted Data).

Returns:

The fitted model.

Return type:

ParametricRegressionModel

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import Weibull, WeibullAFT
>>> np.random.seed(1)
>>> Z = np.random.binomial(1, 0.5, 100).reshape(-1, 1)
>>> x = Weibull.random(100, 10, 2) * np.exp(-0.5 * Z[:, 0])
>>> model = WeibullAFT.fit(x, Z)
>>> model.params.round(3)
array([9.629, 1.751, 0.473])
fit_from_df(df: pd.DataFrame, x_col: str | None = None, Z_cols: str | list[str] | None = None, c_col: str | None = None, n_col: str | None = None, tl_col: str | None = None, tr_col: str | None = None, xl_col: str | None = None, xr_col: str | None = None, formula: str | None = None, init: npt.ArrayLike | None = None, fixed: dict[str, float] | None = None, center: bool = False, w_col: str | None = None, *, unit=None) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit the regression model using a pandas DataFrame as the input.

The names of the covariates are retained on the fitted model so that a DataFrame can later be passed to the prediction methods (sf, ff, df, hf, Hf, random) and the correct columns will be selected automatically.

Parameters:

  • df (pandas.DataFrame) – The dataframe containing the data.

  • x_col (str, optional) – The column name of the observed times. Required unless xl_col and xr_col are given.

  • Z_cols (str or list of str, optional) – The column name(s) of the covariates. Mutually exclusive with formula.

  • c_col (str, optional) – The column name of the censoring indicator.

  • n_col (str, optional) – The column name of the number of observations at each time.

  • tl_col (str, optional) – The column name of the left truncation values.

  • tr_col (str, optional) – The column name of the right truncation values.

  • xl_col (str, optional) – The column names of the left and right ends of each observation’s interval, in place of x_col: the two columns of the (N, 2) x that fit() takes for interval censored data, with c_col giving the censoring of each row as for fit() (#571). Given with x_col, each row is an exact time in x_col or a range in these, the other blank; a row giving both is left out, with a warning.

  • xr_col (str, optional) – The column names of the left and right ends of each observation’s interval, in place of x_col: the two columns of the (N, 2) x that fit() takes for interval censored data, with c_col giving the censoring of each row as for fit() (#571). Given with x_col, each row is an exact time in x_col or a range in these, the other blank; a row giving both is left out, with a warning.

  • formula (str, optional) – A formulaic formula describing the covariates, e.g. "age + sex". Mutually exclusive with Z_cols.

  • init (array_like, optional) – The initial values for the parameters.

  • fixed (dict, optional) – A dictionary of parameters to fix to a specific value.

  • center (bool, optional) – Report the baseline at the covariate means (stored as model.center) instead of at Z = 0; see fit. Not available for an accelerated life model.

  • w_col (str, optional) – The column name of the sampling, propensity or censoring weights, passed to fit as w.

Returns:

The fitted model, with feature_names (and formula) set.

Return type:

ParametricRegressionModel

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> from surpyval import Weibull, WeibullPH
>>> np.random.seed(1)
>>> age = np.random.uniform(20, 60, 100)
>>> weight = np.random.uniform(50, 100, 100)
>>> time = Weibull.random(100, 10, 2) * np.exp(-0.02 * (age - 40))
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({
...     "time": time,
...     "age": age,
...     "weight": weight,
...     "censored": np.zeros(100, dtype=int),
... })
>>> model = WeibullPH.fit_from_df(
...     df, x_col="time", Z_cols=["age", "weight"], c_col="censored"
... )
>>> model.feature_names
['age', 'weight']
>>> model.sf([10, 20], df[["age", "weight"]].head(2)).round(4)
array([0.4757, 0.0024])
fit_penalised(x: ArrayLike, Z: ArrayLike, c: ArrayLike | None = None, n: ArrayLike | None = None, t: ArrayLike | None = None, penalizer: float | ArrayLike = 0.1, l1_ratio: float = 0.0, standardise: bool = True, tl: ArrayLike | None = None, tr: ArrayLike | None = None, tol: float = 1e-10, w: ArrayLike | float | None = None, *, unit=None) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit the model with a ridge, lasso or elastic-net penalty on the covariate coefficients (the baseline distribution’s parameters are not penalised): for many covariates, or correlated ones.

The fit minimises the negative log-likelihood divided by the number of units N (the sum of n) plus

\[\sum_j \lambda_j \left( \frac{1 - a}{2} b_j^2 + a |b_j| \right),\]

with \(\lambda_j\) the penalizer and \(a\) the l1_ratio, as lifelines’ penalizer and l1_ratio and glmnet’s lambda and alpha. A lasso or elastic-net penalty sets some coefficients exactly to 0: the L1 part is minimised exactly (each coefficient the difference of two non-negative parts, by L-BFGS-B, then Newton steps on those not at 0 with the optimality conditions of those at 0 checked), not smoothed. model.maximum is "verified" when those conditions hold.

Every kind of censoring and truncation of fit() is taken: left, right and interval censoring, and truncation on the left, the right or both. N counts the rows, weighted by n (and by the weights w, if given). The model predicts as any fitted model does, but has no covariance, standard errors, confidence bounds or p-values: penalised estimates are biased towards 0 by design, and intervals from the penalised curvature would not have their stated coverage; those calls raise an error that says so (its summary() shows them as nan).

Parameters:

  • x (array_like) – As for fit().

  • Z (array_like) – As for fit().

  • c (array_like) – As for fit().

  • n (array_like) – As for fit().

  • t (array_like) – As for fit().

  • tl (array_like) – As for fit().

  • tr (array_like) – As for fit().

  • penalizer (float or array_like, optional) – \(\lambda\): one value, or one per column of Z (0 leaves a coefficient unpenalised). Default 0.1.

  • l1_ratio (float, optional) – \(a\), from 0 (ridge, the default) to 1 (lasso).

  • standardise (bool, optional) – True (the default) penalises the coefficients of the covariates divided by their standard deviations (count-weighted, divisor N, as glmnet), so the penalty does not depend on their units; the coefficients are reported on the covariates’ own scale either way. The divisor is N, not N - 1 (lifelines’), because the objective is glmnet’s, the mean negative log-likelihood plus the penalty; lifelines’ standard deviations are larger by \(\sqrt{N / (N - 1)}\) (0.5% at N = 100, 5% at N = 10), so its penalty is that much stronger. To reproduce a lifelines fit, divide the covariates by their ddof=1 standard deviations yourself and pass standardise=False.

  • tol (float, optional) – The optimality tolerance on the gradient of the objective.

  • w (array_like, optional) – Sampling, propensity or censoring weights, one positive number per row (or one for every row). Each row’s term in the log-likelihood is multiplied by n * w, N is \(N_w = \sum n w\) and the standardisation weights the rows by n * w (divisor \(N_w\), glmnet’s weights), so w and c * w give the same fit. Whole-number weights give the fit of the rows repeated (counts n). As every penalised fit, a weighted one has no standard errors or bounds, and its aic and bic are refused, as for every weighted fit.

Returns:

The fitted model, with penalty recording the penalizer (per column), l1_ratio, standardise and the columns’ scale.

Return type:

ParametricRegressionModel

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import WeibullAFT
>>> rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
>>> Z = rng.normal(size=(200, 5))
>>> x = 10 * rng.weibull(2, 200) * np.exp(-0.5 * Z[:, 0])
>>> model = WeibullAFT.fit_penalised(x, Z, penalizer=0.05, l1_ratio=1)
>>> model.params[2:].round(3)
array([ 0.446, -0.035, -0.007,  0.   ,  0.   ])
fit_tvc(i: ArrayLike, xl: ArrayLike, xr: ArrayLike, c: ArrayLike, Z: ArrayLike, n: ArrayLike | None = None, fixed: dict[str, float] | None = None, center: bool = False) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit the accelerated failure time model to start-stop (counting-process) time-varying-covariate data.

Parameters:

  • i (array_like) – Subject identifier per interval row.

  • xl (array_like) – The open-closed observation interval (xl, xr] of each row.

  • xr (array_like) – The open-closed observation interval (xl, xr] of each row.

  • c (array_like) – Status at xr in surpyval’s convention: 0 terminal event, 1 right-censored interval end (covariate change / exit).

  • Z (array_like) – Covariate row, constant on each interval.

  • n (array_like, optional) – Count weight per subject (read from the terminal row). Default 1.

  • fixed (dict, optional) – Parameters to hold fixed, by name.

  • center (bool, optional) – Report the baseline at the covariate means of the interval rows (stored as model.center) instead of at Z = 0, as for fit().

Returns:

The fitted model, carrying the accumulated-age likelihood so its confidence bounds are correct.

Return type:

ParametricRegressionModel

fit_tvc_from_df(df: Any, i_col: str, xl_col: str, xr_col: str, c_col: str, Z_cols: str | list[str] | None = None, n_col: str | None = None, fixed: dict[str, float] | None = None, center: bool = False, formula: str | None = None) → ParametricRegressionModel

fit_tvc from a start-stop DataFrame. The covariates are Z_cols, a single column name or a list, or instead formula, a formulaic formula as in fit_from_df, which codes categorical columns; give exactly one. feature_names (and the formula and its encoding) are recorded on the model, so it predicts from a DataFrame with the same design. fixed and center are as for fit_tvc().

fit_tvc_penalised(i: ArrayLike, xl: ArrayLike, xr: ArrayLike, c: ArrayLike, Z: ArrayLike, n: ArrayLike | None = None, penalizer: float | ArrayLike = 0.1, l1_ratio: float = 0.0, standardise: bool = True, tol: float = 1e-10, w: ArrayLike | float | None = None) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit the accelerated failure time model to start-stop time-varying-covariate data (as fit_tvc(), on the accumulated-age likelihood) with a ridge, lasso or elastic-net penalty on the coefficients (as fit_penalised).

The objective is fit_penalised’s, with N the number of subjects (each weighted by the n of its last row), the likelihood having one term per subject, and the covariates standardised over the subjects: each subject’s covariate is its average over its follow-up, each row weighted by its length xr - xl. A subject’s accelerated age is the sum over its rows of exp(beta'z) (xr - xl), so splitting a row into several with the same covariates leaves the likelihood, N and the scale, and so the fit, unchanged. The model has no covariance, standard errors, bounds or tests (see fit_penalised).

Parameters:

  • i (array_like) – As for fit_tvc() (each subject’s rows tile its follow-up from 0).

  • xl (array_like) – As for fit_tvc() (each subject’s rows tile its follow-up from 0).

  • xr (array_like) – As for fit_tvc() (each subject’s rows tile its follow-up from 0).

  • c (array_like) – As for fit_tvc() (each subject’s rows tile its follow-up from 0).

  • Z (array_like) – As for fit_tvc() (each subject’s rows tile its follow-up from 0).

  • n (array_like) – As for fit_tvc() (each subject’s rows tile its follow-up from 0).

  • penalizer – As for fit_penalised.

  • l1_ratio – As for fit_penalised.

  • standardise – As for fit_penalised.

  • tol – As for fit_penalised.

  • w (None) – Weights are refused: fit_tvc() takes none either.

Returns:

The fitted model, with is_tvc and penalty set.

Return type:

ParametricRegressionModel

Examples

Each unit runs at its own stress z, which steps up by 0.5 half way through its life; two other covariates do nothing:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import WeibullAFT
>>> rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
>>> z = rng.normal(size=200)
>>> T = rng.weibull(2.0, 200) * 5 * np.exp(-0.5 * z)
>>> other = rng.normal(size=(200, 2))
>>> i = np.repeat(np.arange(200), 2)
>>> xl = np.column_stack([0 * T, T / 2]).ravel()
>>> xr = np.column_stack([T / 2, T]).ravel()
>>> c = np.tile([1, 0], 200)
>>> Z = np.column_stack(
...     [np.column_stack([z, z + 0.5]).ravel(), other[i]]
... )
>>> model = WeibullAFT.fit_tvc_penalised(
...     i, xl, xr, c, Z, penalizer=0.05, l1_ratio=1
... )
>>> model.params.round(3)
array([ 5.502,  1.943,  0.585, -0.066,  0.   ])
fit_tvc_timeline(i: ArrayLike, x: ArrayLike, Z: ArrayLike, c: ArrayLike, n: ArrayLike | None = None, fixed: dict[str, float] | None = None, center: bool = False) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit from a per-subject covariate timeline (one row per covariate change, terminal status on the last row) instead of explicit (xl, xr] intervals. See CoxPH.fit_tvc_timeline for the format. fixed and center are as for fit_tvc().

fit_tvc_timeline_from_df(df: Any, i_col: str, x_col: str, Z_cols: str | list[str] | None, c_col: str, n_col: str | None = None, fixed: dict[str, float] | None = None, center: bool = False, formula: str | None = None) → ParametricRegressionModel

fit_tvc_timeline() from a covariate-timeline DataFrame, as for the proportional hazards models and Cox.

i_col, x_col, c_col and n_col name the columns passed to fit_tvc_timeline() as i, x, c and n. The covariates are Z_cols, a column name or a list of them, or instead (pass Z_cols=None) formula, as for fit_tvc_from_df(); the model records feature_names (and the formula and its encoding). fixed and center are as for fit_tvc(). The timeline is the same data as its start-stop rows, so the fit is that of fit_tvc_from_df().

Examples

Each unit runs at its own stress z, which steps up by 0.5 half way through its life; the last row of a unit gives its exit time and status:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> from surpyval import WeibullAFT
>>> rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
>>> z = rng.normal(size=100)
>>> T = rng.weibull(2.0, 100) * 5 * np.exp(-0.5 * z)
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({
...     "id": np.repeat(np.arange(100), 3),
...     "time": np.column_stack([0 * T, T / 2, T]).ravel(),
...     "z": np.column_stack([z, z + 0.5, z + 0.5]).ravel(),
...     "c": 0,
... })
>>> model = WeibullAFT.fit_tvc_timeline_from_df(
...     df, "id", "time", "z", "c"
... )
>>> model.feature_names
['z']
fit_tvc_timeline_penalised(i: ArrayLike, x: ArrayLike, Z: ArrayLike, c: ArrayLike, n: ArrayLike | None = None, penalizer: float | ArrayLike = 0.1, l1_ratio: float = 0.0, standardise: bool = True, tol: float = 1e-10, w: ArrayLike | float | None = None) → ParametricRegressionModel

fit_tvc_timeline() with a ridge, lasso or elastic-net penalty: the timeline is expanded to start-stop rows and fitted by fit_tvc_penalised(), so it gives the same fit as the equivalent start-stop data.

Parameters:

  • i (array_like) – As for fit_tvc_timeline().

  • x (array_like) – As for fit_tvc_timeline().

  • Z (array_like) – As for fit_tvc_timeline().

  • c (array_like) – As for fit_tvc_timeline().

  • n (array_like) – As for fit_tvc_timeline().

  • penalizer – As for fit_tvc_penalised().

  • l1_ratio – As for fit_tvc_penalised().

  • standardise – As for fit_tvc_penalised().

  • tol – As for fit_tvc_penalised().

  • w – As for fit_tvc_penalised().

Returns:

The fitted model, with is_tvc and penalty set.

Return type:

ParametricRegressionModel

fitter_kind: str = 'accelerated failure time fitter'

The repr (#614)

hf(x: NDArray | float, Z: NDArray | float, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

Hazard rate \(e^{\beta' Z} h_0(e^{\beta' Z} x)\) at x for covariates Z; params as for Hf().

name_suffix: str = 'AFT'

The end of the public name of a family’s fitter after its distribution’s, for a fitter without a name (WeibullAFT).

neg_ll(data: SurpyvalData, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

The negative log-likelihood of data at params (the distribution parameters followed by the covariate parameters), for every kind of censoring and truncation.

random(size: int, Z: ArrayLike, *params: float, random_state: Any = None) → tuple[NDArray, NDArray]

Draw size samples for each covariate row of Z.

S(x | Z) = S0(phi x), so a draw U of the survival is reached at x = q / phi, where q is the baseline’s time with survival U (on a baseline over the whole real line, q and so the draw can be below 0). Returns the draws and a 2-D array of the covariate row each was drawn at, row by row, as the proportional hazards random. random_state seeds the draw: None (the default) draws from numpy’s global generator, so np.random.seed reproduces it; an int or a numpy.random.Generator gives a stream of its own.

Examples

A unit with Z = 1 and beta = 0.5 ages e^0.5 times as fast, so its median life is the baseline’s divided by e^0.5:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import Weibull, WeibullAFT
>>> x, Z = WeibullAFT.random(20000, [[1.0]], 10.0, 2.0, 0.5,
...                          random_state=1)
>>> float(np.median(x).round(2))
5.06
>>> float((Weibull.qf(0.5, 10.0, 2.0) / np.exp(0.5)).round(2))
5.05
sf(x: NDArray | float, Z: NDArray | float, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

Survival function at x for covariates Z, \(R(x \mid Z) = e^{-H(x \mid Z)}\).

params are the distribution parameters followed by the covariate coefficients, in the order of a fitted model’s params. A fitted model’s own sf(x, Z) supplies them.

Proportional Odds (PO)

\[\frac{S(x \mid Z)}{F(x \mid Z)} = \frac{S_0(x)}{F_0(x)} \cdot e^{\beta'Z}\]

Pre-built instances: ExponentialPO, NormalPO, WeibullPO, GumbelPO, LogisticPO, LogNormalPO, GammaPO.

surpyval.univariate.regression.proportional_odds.proportional_odds_fitter.PO(distribution: Any) → ProportionalOddsFitter

Create a Proportional Odds fitter for the given distribution.

Uses exp(beta’Z) as the odds multiplier — the standard parameterisation for proportional odds survival models.

Parameters:

distribution (ParametricFitter) – A surpyval parametric distribution (e.g. Logistic, LogLogistic).

Returns:

A configured fitter with a .fit(x, Z, ...) method.

Return type:

ProportionalOddsFitter

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import Logistic
>>> from surpyval import PO
>>> np.random.seed(1)
>>> Z = np.random.binomial(1, 0.5, 100).reshape(-1, 1)
>>> x = Logistic.random(100, 10, 2) + 2.0 * Z[:, 0]
>>> model = PO(Logistic).fit(x, Z=Z)
>>> model.params.round(3)
array([9.708, 2.337, 0.918])
class surpyval.univariate.regression.proportional_odds.proportional_odds_fitter.ProportionalOddsFitter(distribution: Any)

Bases: TVCFitMixin, LogLinearRegressionFitter

Proportional Odds model fitter using \(\phi = e^{\beta' Z}\) as the multiplier of the survival odds \(O(x) = S(x) / F(x)\):

\[O(x \mid Z) = \phi\, O_0(x), \qquad S(x \mid Z) = \frac{\phi S_0(x)}{F_0(x) + \phi S_0(x)}, \qquad h(x \mid Z) = \frac{h_0(x)}{F_0(x) + \phi S_0(x)}.\]

A positive beta coefficient means higher covariate values increase the survival odds (protective effect – longer life). This is the opposite sign to the PH and AFT fitters, where a positive coefficient shortens life; negate the coefficients to compare them.

The hazard depends only on the time and the current covariate, so a fitted model is evaluated exactly along a step covariate path by sf_tvc / Hf_tvc (a sum of per-segment cumulative-hazard increments), and fit_tvc (with the timeline and DataFrame variants) fits start-stop time-varying-covariate data exactly by splitting each subject into one delayed-entry row per constant-covariate interval, as for the proportional and additive hazards fitters.

Use the pre-built instances (LogisticPO, WeibullPO, …) or the PO factory.

Hf(x: NDArray | float, Z: NDArray | float, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

Cumulative hazard \(-\ln S(x \mid Z)\) at x for covariates Z; params as for sf().

Evaluated as \(\ln(1 + F_0 / (\phi S_0))\), which keeps full relative precision where the cumulative hazard is small (#528), and where \(\phi S_0\) is below the normal range as \(H_0(x) - \ln\phi + \ln(1 + (\phi - 1) S_0)\), which stays finite there (-log(sf) is inf, and a difference of two such values along a time-varying path would be nan).

df(x: NDArray | float, Z: NDArray | float, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

Density \(\phi f_0 / (F_0 + \phi S_0)^2\) at x for covariates Z; params as for sf().

ff(x: NDArray | float, Z: NDArray | float, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

Failure (CDF) function \(F_0 / (F_0 + \phi S_0)\) at x for covariates Z; params as for sf().

fit(x: ArrayLike, Z: ArrayLike, c: ArrayLike | None = None, n: ArrayLike | None = None, t: ArrayLike | None = None, init: ArrayLike | None = None, fixed: dict[str, float] | None = None, center: bool = False, tl: ArrayLike | None = None, tr: ArrayLike | None = None, w: ArrayLike | float | None = None, *, unit=None) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit the proportional odds model by maximum likelihood.

Parameters:

  • x (array_like) – The observed event times.

  • Z (array_like) – The covariate matrix, one row per observation (a 1-D array is read as a single covariate). Rows with a missing or infinite covariate are dropped, with a warning.

  • c (array_like, optional) – The censoring indicators (0 observed, 1 right, -1 left, 2 interval). Defaults to all observed.

  • n (array_like, optional) – The count of observations at each time. Defaults to 1.

  • t (array_like, optional) – Truncation bounds: an (N, 2) array of the left and right truncation times of each observation.

  • tl (array_like or float, optional) – The left / right truncation times of each observation (or one for every observation), the columns of t, which they replace (#662).

  • tr (array_like or float, optional) – The left / right truncation times of each observation (or one for every observation), the columns of t, which they replace (#662).

  • init (array_like, optional) – Initial parameter values: the distribution parameters followed by the covariate coefficients.

  • fixed (dict, optional) – Parameters to hold fixed, by name (a distribution parameter such as "beta", or a coefficient: its covariate’s column name, else "coef_0", …).

  • center (bool, optional) – False (the default) reports the baseline at Z = 0. True reports the baseline at the covariate means (stored as model.center) instead: the fit runs on Z - center, and init and fixed are read there too. Use it for covariates far from 0 (a year, a date), where the baseline at Z = 0 cannot be represented or fitted, which the default fit refuses with a ValueError saying so.

  • w (array_like or float, optional) – Sampling, propensity or censoring weights, one positive number per row (beside its count n). The fit maximises the weighted (pseudo) likelihood and covariance(), behind every Wald bound, is the robust (sandwich) covariance, as R’s survreg(..., weights = w, robust = TRUE); the likelihood-ratio and bootstrap bounds and the information criteria refuse (see Weighted Data).

Returns:

The fitted model.

Return type:

ParametricRegressionModel

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import Logistic, LogisticPO
>>> np.random.seed(1)
>>> Z = np.random.binomial(1, 0.5, 100).reshape(-1, 1)
>>> x = Logistic.random(100, 10, 2) + 2.0 * Z[:, 0]
>>> model = LogisticPO.fit(x, Z)
>>> model.params.round(3)
array([9.708, 2.337, 0.918])
fit_from_df(df: pd.DataFrame, x_col: str | None = None, Z_cols: str | list[str] | None = None, c_col: str | None = None, n_col: str | None = None, tl_col: str | None = None, tr_col: str | None = None, xl_col: str | None = None, xr_col: str | None = None, formula: str | None = None, init: npt.ArrayLike | None = None, fixed: dict[str, float] | None = None, center: bool = False, w_col: str | None = None, *, unit=None) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit the regression model using a pandas DataFrame as the input.

The names of the covariates are retained on the fitted model so that a DataFrame can later be passed to the prediction methods (sf, ff, df, hf, Hf, random) and the correct columns will be selected automatically.

Parameters:

  • df (pandas.DataFrame) – The dataframe containing the data.

  • x_col (str, optional) – The column name of the observed times. Required unless xl_col and xr_col are given.

  • Z_cols (str or list of str, optional) – The column name(s) of the covariates. Mutually exclusive with formula.

  • c_col (str, optional) – The column name of the censoring indicator.

  • n_col (str, optional) – The column name of the number of observations at each time.

  • tl_col (str, optional) – The column name of the left truncation values.

  • tr_col (str, optional) – The column name of the right truncation values.

  • xl_col (str, optional) – The column names of the left and right ends of each observation’s interval, in place of x_col: the two columns of the (N, 2) x that fit() takes for interval censored data, with c_col giving the censoring of each row as for fit() (#571). Given with x_col, each row is an exact time in x_col or a range in these, the other blank; a row giving both is left out, with a warning.

  • xr_col (str, optional) – The column names of the left and right ends of each observation’s interval, in place of x_col: the two columns of the (N, 2) x that fit() takes for interval censored data, with c_col giving the censoring of each row as for fit() (#571). Given with x_col, each row is an exact time in x_col or a range in these, the other blank; a row giving both is left out, with a warning.

  • formula (str, optional) – A formulaic formula describing the covariates, e.g. "age + sex". Mutually exclusive with Z_cols.

  • init (array_like, optional) – The initial values for the parameters.

  • fixed (dict, optional) – A dictionary of parameters to fix to a specific value.

  • center (bool, optional) – Report the baseline at the covariate means (stored as model.center) instead of at Z = 0; see fit. Not available for an accelerated life model.

  • w_col (str, optional) – The column name of the sampling, propensity or censoring weights, passed to fit as w.

Returns:

The fitted model, with feature_names (and formula) set.

Return type:

ParametricRegressionModel

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> from surpyval import Weibull, WeibullPH
>>> np.random.seed(1)
>>> age = np.random.uniform(20, 60, 100)
>>> weight = np.random.uniform(50, 100, 100)
>>> time = Weibull.random(100, 10, 2) * np.exp(-0.02 * (age - 40))
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({
...     "time": time,
...     "age": age,
...     "weight": weight,
...     "censored": np.zeros(100, dtype=int),
... })
>>> model = WeibullPH.fit_from_df(
...     df, x_col="time", Z_cols=["age", "weight"], c_col="censored"
... )
>>> model.feature_names
['age', 'weight']
>>> model.sf([10, 20], df[["age", "weight"]].head(2)).round(4)
array([0.4757, 0.0024])
fit_penalised(x: ArrayLike, Z: ArrayLike, c: ArrayLike | None = None, n: ArrayLike | None = None, t: ArrayLike | None = None, penalizer: float | ArrayLike = 0.1, l1_ratio: float = 0.0, standardise: bool = True, tl: ArrayLike | None = None, tr: ArrayLike | None = None, tol: float = 1e-10, w: ArrayLike | float | None = None, *, unit=None) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit the model with a ridge, lasso or elastic-net penalty on the covariate coefficients (the baseline distribution’s parameters are not penalised): for many covariates, or correlated ones.

The fit minimises the negative log-likelihood divided by the number of units N (the sum of n) plus

\[\sum_j \lambda_j \left( \frac{1 - a}{2} b_j^2 + a |b_j| \right),\]

with \(\lambda_j\) the penalizer and \(a\) the l1_ratio, as lifelines’ penalizer and l1_ratio and glmnet’s lambda and alpha. A lasso or elastic-net penalty sets some coefficients exactly to 0: the L1 part is minimised exactly (each coefficient the difference of two non-negative parts, by L-BFGS-B, then Newton steps on those not at 0 with the optimality conditions of those at 0 checked), not smoothed. model.maximum is "verified" when those conditions hold.

Every kind of censoring and truncation of fit() is taken: left, right and interval censoring, and truncation on the left, the right or both. N counts the rows, weighted by n (and by the weights w, if given). The model predicts as any fitted model does, but has no covariance, standard errors, confidence bounds or p-values: penalised estimates are biased towards 0 by design, and intervals from the penalised curvature would not have their stated coverage; those calls raise an error that says so (its summary() shows them as nan).

Parameters:

  • x (array_like) – As for fit().

  • Z (array_like) – As for fit().

  • c (array_like) – As for fit().

  • n (array_like) – As for fit().

  • t (array_like) – As for fit().

  • tl (array_like) – As for fit().

  • tr (array_like) – As for fit().

  • penalizer (float or array_like, optional) – \(\lambda\): one value, or one per column of Z (0 leaves a coefficient unpenalised). Default 0.1.

  • l1_ratio (float, optional) – \(a\), from 0 (ridge, the default) to 1 (lasso).

  • standardise (bool, optional) – True (the default) penalises the coefficients of the covariates divided by their standard deviations (count-weighted, divisor N, as glmnet), so the penalty does not depend on their units; the coefficients are reported on the covariates’ own scale either way. The divisor is N, not N - 1 (lifelines’), because the objective is glmnet’s, the mean negative log-likelihood plus the penalty; lifelines’ standard deviations are larger by \(\sqrt{N / (N - 1)}\) (0.5% at N = 100, 5% at N = 10), so its penalty is that much stronger. To reproduce a lifelines fit, divide the covariates by their ddof=1 standard deviations yourself and pass standardise=False.

  • tol (float, optional) – The optimality tolerance on the gradient of the objective.

  • w (array_like, optional) – Sampling, propensity or censoring weights, one positive number per row (or one for every row). Each row’s term in the log-likelihood is multiplied by n * w, N is \(N_w = \sum n w\) and the standardisation weights the rows by n * w (divisor \(N_w\), glmnet’s weights), so w and c * w give the same fit. Whole-number weights give the fit of the rows repeated (counts n). As every penalised fit, a weighted one has no standard errors or bounds, and its aic and bic are refused, as for every weighted fit.

Returns:

The fitted model, with penalty recording the penalizer (per column), l1_ratio, standardise and the columns’ scale.

Return type:

ParametricRegressionModel

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import WeibullAFT
>>> rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
>>> Z = rng.normal(size=(200, 5))
>>> x = 10 * rng.weibull(2, 200) * np.exp(-0.5 * Z[:, 0])
>>> model = WeibullAFT.fit_penalised(x, Z, penalizer=0.05, l1_ratio=1)
>>> model.params[2:].round(3)
array([ 0.446, -0.035, -0.007,  0.   ,  0.   ])
fit_tvc(i: npt.ArrayLike, xl: npt.ArrayLike, xr: npt.ArrayLike, c: npt.ArrayLike, Z: npt.ArrayLike, n: npt.ArrayLike | None = None, **kwargs: Any) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit the model to time-varying covariates in start-stop format.

Each row is one observation interval (xl, xr] of subject i on which the covariate row Z is constant; c is 0 (event at xr) only on the interval that ends at the subject’s event and 1 (right-censored) otherwise – surpyval’s censoring convention. The intervals are validated and mapped to left-truncated observations (t = [xl, inf]), then fitted with the ordinary parametric MLE, so the fit is identical to the equivalent non-time-varying data and its log-likelihood is that of sf_tvc / hf along each subject’s covariate path. Extra keyword arguments (init, fixed, center) are passed through to fit.

A subject’s rows must not overlap, it may have at most one event, and that event must be on its last interval; gaps between its intervals (not at risk) and delayed entry (a first xl > 0) are allowed.

A subject’s first row enters at its xl, as any other row does (#952). For a baseline that starts at 0, entering at 0 is no truncation. For one defined below 0 (Normal, Gumbel, Logistic) a first xl of 0 means the subject entered at 0, and the fit conditions on its surviving to 0; give -inf for a subject followed since -inf, its first covariate row holding since then.

Parameters:

  • i (array_like) – Subject identifier of each interval row.

  • xl (array_like) – The open-closed interval (xl, xr] of each row.

  • xr (array_like) – The open-closed interval (xl, xr] of each row.

  • c (array_like) – Status at xr: 0 for the subject’s event, 1 for a right-censored interval end (a covariate change or the end of follow-up).

  • Z (array_like) – The covariate row in force on each interval (a 1-D array is a single covariate).

  • n (array_like, optional) – Count weight of each row. Defaults to 1.

  • **kwargs – Passed to fit (init, fixed, center).

Returns:

The fitted model, with is_tvc set. Evaluate it along a covariate path with sf_tvc / Hf_tvc.

Return type:

ParametricRegressionModel

Examples

Units fail at rate 0.5 until a stress switches on at a random time, and at 0.5 e after it; a unit that outlives its switch contributes two rows:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import WeibullPH
>>> rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
>>> n = 300
>>> switch = rng.uniform(0.3, 1.5, n)
>>> t_low = rng.exponential(2.0, n)
>>> t_high = switch + rng.exponential(2.0 / np.e, n)
>>> T = np.where(t_low > switch, t_high, t_low)
>>> one = T <= switch
>>> i = np.r_[np.arange(n), np.flatnonzero(~one)]
>>> xl = np.r_[np.zeros(n), switch[~one]]
>>> xr = np.r_[np.where(one, T, switch), T[~one]]
>>> c = np.r_[np.where(one, 0, 1), np.zeros((~one).sum(), dtype=int)]
>>> Z = np.r_[np.zeros(n), np.ones((~one).sum())]
>>> model = WeibullPH.fit_tvc(i, xl, xr, c, Z)
>>> model.params.round(3)  # alpha, beta (shape), coef_0
array([2.059, 0.992, 0.995])

The survival of a unit whose stress switches on at time 1:

>>> model.sf_tvc([1.0, 2.0], [[0.0], [1.0]], xl=[0.0, 1.0]).round(4)
array([0.6136, 0.1661])
fit_tvc_from_df(df: pd.DataFrame, i_col: str, xl_col: str, xr_col: str, c_col: str, Z_cols: str | list[str] | None = None, n_col: str | None = None, formula: str | None = None, **kwargs: Any) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit start-stop time-varying-covariate data from a DataFrame.

i_col, xl_col, xr_col, c_col and n_col name the columns passed to fit_tvc() as i, xl, xr, c and n. The covariates are Z_cols, a column name or a list of them, or instead formula, a formulaic formula as in fit_from_df, which codes categorical (e.g. "yes" / "no") columns; give exactly one. The model records feature_names (and the formula and its encoding), so it predicts from a DataFrame with the same design. Other keyword arguments go to fit (init, fixed, center). Returns the fitted ParametricRegressionModel.

Examples

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> from surpyval import WeibullPH
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({
...     "id": [0, 0, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6],
...     "start": [0, 2, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 3, 0, 0],
...     "stop": [2, 5, 3, 1, 4, 6, 3, 7, 2, 8],
...     "c": [1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1],
...     "dose": ["low", "high", "low", "low", "high", "low", "low",
...              "high", "high", "low"],
... })
>>> model = WeibullPH.fit_tvc_from_df(
...     df, "id", "start", "stop", "c", formula="dose"
... )
>>> model.feature_names
['dose[T.low]']
fit_tvc_penalised(i: npt.ArrayLike, xl: npt.ArrayLike, xr: npt.ArrayLike, c: npt.ArrayLike, Z: npt.ArrayLike, n: npt.ArrayLike | None = None, penalizer: float | npt.ArrayLike = 0.1, l1_ratio: float = 0.0, standardise: bool = True, tol: float = 1e-10, w: npt.ArrayLike | float | None = None) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit the model to time-varying covariates in start-stop format (as fit_tvc()) with a ridge, lasso or elastic-net penalty on the coefficients (as fit_penalised).

The rows are validated and fitted as the delayed-entry rows fit_tvc() fits, by fit_penalised’s objective, with N the number of subjects (the distinct i, each weighted by the n of its last row), not of rows, and the covariates standardised over the subjects: each subject’s covariate is its average over its follow-up, each row weighted by its length xr - xl. Splitting a subject’s follow-up into more rows with the same covariates leaves the likelihood unchanged (the cumulative hazard is additive over the rows), and so, with N and the scale per subject, it leaves the fit unchanged too, as for CoxPH.fit_tvc_penalised. The model has no covariance, standard errors, bounds or tests (see fit_penalised).

The parametric additive hazards models (WeibullAH, …) have no penalised fit, with or without time-varying covariates, and refuse: their coefficients are rates, so a penalty on them would depend on the unit of time.

Parameters:

  • i (array_like) – As for fit_tvc().

  • xl (array_like) – As for fit_tvc().

  • xr (array_like) – As for fit_tvc().

  • c (array_like) – As for fit_tvc().

  • Z (array_like) – As for fit_tvc().

  • n (array_like) – As for fit_tvc().

  • penalizer – As for fit_penalised.

  • l1_ratio – As for fit_penalised.

  • standardise – As for fit_penalised.

  • tol – As for fit_penalised.

  • w (None) – Weights are refused here: give them to fit_penalised on rows without time-varying covariates, or to the unpenalised fit_tvc().

Returns:

The fitted model, with is_tvc and penalty set.

Return type:

ParametricRegressionModel

Examples

Units fail at rate 0.5 until a stress switches on at a random time, and at 0.5 e after it; two other covariates do nothing:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import WeibullPH
>>> rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
>>> n = 300
>>> switch = rng.uniform(0.3, 1.5, n)
>>> t_low = rng.exponential(2.0, n)
>>> t_high = switch + rng.exponential(2.0 / np.e, n)
>>> T = np.where(t_low > switch, t_high, t_low)
>>> one = T <= switch
>>> i = np.r_[np.arange(n), np.flatnonzero(~one)]
>>> xl = np.r_[np.zeros(n), switch[~one]]
>>> xr = np.r_[np.where(one, T, switch), T[~one]]
>>> c = np.r_[np.where(one, 0, 1), np.zeros((~one).sum(), dtype=int)]
>>> stress = np.r_[np.zeros(n), np.ones((~one).sum())]
>>> Z = np.column_stack([stress, rng.normal(size=(n, 2))[i]])
>>> model = WeibullPH.fit_tvc_penalised(
...     i, xl, xr, c, Z, penalizer=0.05, l1_ratio=1
... )
>>> model.params.round(3)  # alpha, beta (shape), coefficients
array([1.928, 1.032, 0.895, 0.087, 0.   ])
fit_tvc_timeline(i: npt.ArrayLike, x: npt.ArrayLike, Z: npt.ArrayLike, c: npt.ArrayLike, n: npt.ArrayLike | None = None, **kwargs: Any) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit the model from a covariate timeline (the xicnt-style input).

Each subject’s rows give its covariate history: a value Z takes effect at time x and holds until the subject’s next row, with the terminal event / censoring on the last row’s c (0 event, 1 censored). The timeline is expanded to start-stop intervals and fitted as fit_tvc(), so the fit is identical to the equivalent start-stop data.

Parameters:

  • i (array_like) – Subject identifier of each timeline row.

  • x (array_like) – The time each row’s covariate value takes effect, strictly increasing within a subject: the first is the entry time, the last the event or censoring time.

  • Z (array_like) – The covariate row in force from x; the value on a subject’s last row is ignored.

  • c (array_like) – Status, read from each subject’s last row only (0 event, 1 censored).

  • n (array_like, optional) – Count weight of each subject, read from its last row.

  • **kwargs – Passed to fit (init, fixed, center).

Returns:

The fitted model, with is_tvc set.

Return type:

ParametricRegressionModel

fit_tvc_timeline_from_df(df: pd.DataFrame, i_col: str, x_col: str, Z_cols: str | list[str] | None, c_col: str, n_col: str | None = None, formula: str | None = None, **kwargs: Any) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit a covariate timeline from a DataFrame.

i_col, x_col, c_col and n_col name the columns passed to fit_tvc_timeline() as i, x, c and n. The covariates are Z_cols, a column name or a list of them, or instead (pass Z_cols=None) formula, as for fit_tvc_from_df(); the model records feature_names (and the formula and its encoding). Other keyword arguments go to fit (init, fixed, center). Returns the fitted ParametricRegressionModel.

fit_tvc_timeline_penalised(i: npt.ArrayLike, x: npt.ArrayLike, Z: npt.ArrayLike, c: npt.ArrayLike, n: npt.ArrayLike | None = None, penalizer: float | npt.ArrayLike = 0.1, l1_ratio: float = 0.0, standardise: bool = True, tol: float = 1e-10, w: npt.ArrayLike | float | None = None) → ParametricRegressionModel

fit_tvc_timeline() with a ridge, lasso or elastic-net penalty: the timeline is expanded to start-stop rows and fitted by fit_tvc_penalised(), so it gives the same fit as the equivalent start-stop data.

Parameters:

  • i (array_like) – As for fit_tvc_timeline().

  • x (array_like) – As for fit_tvc_timeline().

  • Z (array_like) – As for fit_tvc_timeline().

  • c (array_like) – As for fit_tvc_timeline().

  • n (array_like) – As for fit_tvc_timeline().

  • penalizer – As for fit_tvc_penalised().

  • l1_ratio – As for fit_tvc_penalised().

  • standardise – As for fit_tvc_penalised().

  • tol – As for fit_tvc_penalised().

  • w – As for fit_tvc_penalised().

Returns:

The fitted model, with is_tvc and penalty set.

Return type:

ParametricRegressionModel

fitter_kind: str = 'proportional odds fitter'

The repr (#614)

hf(x: NDArray | float, Z: NDArray | float, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

Hazard rate \(h_0 / (F_0 + \phi S_0)\) at x for covariates Z; params as for sf().

log_sf(x: NDArray | float, Z: NDArray | float, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

Log of the survival function, \(-H(x \mid Z)\); see Hf().

name_suffix: str = 'PO'

The end of the public name of a family’s fitter after its distribution’s, for a fitter without a name (WeibullAFT).

neg_ll(data: SurpyvalData, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

The negative log-likelihood of data at params (the distribution parameters followed by the covariate parameters), for every kind of censoring and truncation.

random(size: int, Z: ArrayLike, *params: float, random_state: Any = None) → tuple[NDArray, NDArray]

Draw size samples for each covariate row of Z.

The odds of surviving are phi times the baseline’s, so a draw U of the survival is reached where the baseline’s survival is S0 = U / (U + phi (1 - U)), at the baseline cumulative hazard log(1 + phi (1 - U) / U), which the baseline inverts. Returns the draws and a 2-D array of the covariate row each was drawn at, row by row, as the proportional hazards random. random_state seeds the draw: None (the default) draws from numpy’s global generator, so np.random.seed reproduces it; an int or a numpy.random.Generator gives a stream of its own.

Examples

With Z = 1 and beta = 0.5 the odds of surviving to the baseline’s median are e^0.5 to 1, so sf there is e^0.5 / (1 + e^0.5), about 0.622, and so is the share of the draws beyond it:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import Weibull, WeibullPO
>>> x, Z = WeibullPO.random(20000, [[1.0]], 10.0, 2.0, 0.5,
...                         random_state=1)
>>> float(np.mean(x > Weibull.qf(0.5, 10.0, 2.0)).round(3))
0.625
sf(x: NDArray | float, Z: NDArray | float, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

Survival function \(\phi S_0 / (F_0 + \phi S_0)\) at x for covariates Z; params are the distribution parameters followed by the covariate coefficients.

Additive Hazards (AH)

\[h(x \mid Z) = h_0(x) + \beta'Z, \qquad H(x \mid Z) = H_0(x) + x\,\beta'Z\]

The fully parametric counterpart of the semi-parametric Lin-Ying model (Semi-Parametric Additive Hazards). Nothing keeps the hazard positive, so the fit only accepts parameters that keep it positive at every observed failure. When the data would prefer a negative hazard (a strongly protective covariate) it returns the best model on that boundary and warns; it raises only if the optimiser cannot end at a positive-hazard point.

The model is a distribution only where the hazard and the cumulative hazard are both non-negative: at a covariate row its support starts where \(H(x \mid Z)\) reaches 0. That is below 0 for a row with \(\beta'Z > 0\) on a baseline over the whole real line (Normal, Gumbel, Logistic), so such data, negative times and all, are fitted from there; and it is after 0 for a protective row on a baseline whose hazard starts at 0. The fit keeps every observed point inside the support; a fit that ends against that limit (\(H = 0\) at an observation) warns, as one held at a threshold would, and its standard errors are approximate. Predictions outside the support are nan, with a warning.

Pre-built instances: ExponentialAH, NormalAH, WeibullAH, GumbelAH, LogisticAH, LogNormalAH, GammaAH.

surpyval.univariate.regression.additive_hazards.AH(distribution: Any) → AdditiveHazardsFitter

Create a parametric Additive Hazards fitter for the given distribution.

Fits h(x | Z) = h_0(x) + beta'Z – the covariate is a risk difference added to a parametric baseline hazard, rather than a multiplier as in the proportional hazards models.

Parameters:

distribution (ParametricFitter) – A surpyval parametric distribution (e.g. Weibull, Exponential).

Returns:

A configured fitter with a .fit(x, Z, ...) method.

Return type:

AdditiveHazardsFitter

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import Weibull, AH
>>> np.random.seed(1)
>>> Z = np.random.binomial(1, 0.5, 100).reshape(-1, 1)
>>> x = Weibull.random(100, 10, 2) * np.exp(-0.5 * Z[:, 0])
>>> model = AH(Weibull).fit(x, Z=Z)
>>> model.params.round(3)
array([9.332, 1.851, 0.086])
class surpyval.univariate.regression.additive_hazards.additive_hazards_fitter.AdditiveHazardsFitter(name: str, dist: Any)

Bases: HazardIdentitiesMixin, TVCFitMixin, RegressionFitter

Parametric additive hazards fitter: the covariates add a constant risk difference to a parametric baseline hazard,

\[h(x \mid Z) = h_0(x) + \beta' Z, \qquad H(x \mid Z) = H_0(x) + x\, \beta' Z.\]

Use the pre-built instances (WeibullAH, ExponentialAH, …) or the AH factory. The model is a distribution where the hazard and its integral are non-negative, and the fit keeps every observed point there (#828): when the data press against that limit – the hazard nearly zero at a failure, or H zero at an observation – the fit ends on the boundary and warns. Predictions outside the support are nan. A proportional hazards model, which keeps the hazard positive by construction, is the safer choice for strongly protective covariates.

BOUNDARY_INFORMATION_SHARE = 0.5

The share of the information about beta a single failure must carry, and the fraction of its baseline hazard its hazard must be below, for the fit to count as held at the positivity boundary (see _warn_if_on_positivity_boundary).

GRADIENT_FIRST_BUDGET = 400

Gradients the search on the exact gradient may take before the fit falls back to its derivative-free search (see _gradient_first).

Hf(x: NDArray | float, Z: NDArray | float, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

Cumulative hazard \(H_0(x) + x \beta' Z\) at x for covariates Z; params as for hf().

SUPPORT_BOUNDARY_FRACTION = 1e-06

A fit is on the support boundary where H (or h, at an observed time) is below this fraction of the baseline’s at an observed point: the covariate term has cancelled the baseline there. Fits pressed against the boundary leave about 1e-8 of it; one inside it, far more (the smallest share on the regression test fixture’s interior fits is 0.15).

static create(distribution: Any) → AdditiveHazardsFitter

Create a parametric additive hazards fitter for the given distribution.

Parameters:

distribution (ParametricFitter) – A surpyval parametric distribution (e.g. Weibull, Exponential).

Returns:

A configured fitter with a .fit(x, Z, ...) method.

Return type:

AdditiveHazardsFitter

df(x: NDArray | float, Z: NDArray | float, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

Density at x for covariates Z, \(f(x \mid Z) = h(x \mid Z) e^{-H(x \mid Z)}\). params as for sf().

Far in the upper tail, where \(H\) is so large that \(e^{-H}\) underflows to 0, the density is 0, also where the hazard itself has overflowed to inf (a large Weibull shape, or a covariate far from 0): it is not inf * 0 (#714).

ff(x: NDArray | float, Z: NDArray | float, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

Failure (CDF) function at x for covariates Z, \(F(x \mid Z) = 1 - e^{-H(x \mid Z)}\). params as for sf().

fit(x: ArrayLike, Z: ArrayLike, c: ArrayLike | None = None, n: ArrayLike | None = None, t: ArrayLike | None = None, init: ArrayLike | None = None, fixed: dict[str, float] | None = None, center: bool = False, tl: ArrayLike | None = None, tr: ArrayLike | None = None, w: ArrayLike | float | None = None, *, unit=None) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit the parametric additive hazards model by maximum likelihood.

Parameters:

  • x (array_like) – The observed event times.

  • Z (array_like) – The covariate matrix (one row per observation). Rows with a missing or infinite covariate are dropped, with a warning.

  • c (array_like, optional) – The censoring indicators (0 observed, 1 right, -1 left, 2 interval).

  • n (array_like, optional) – The count of observations at each time.

  • t (array_like, optional) – Truncation bounds: an (N, 2) array of the left and right truncation times of each observation.

  • tl (array_like or float, optional) – The left / right truncation times of each observation (or one for every observation), the columns of t, which they replace (#662).

  • tr (array_like or float, optional) – The left / right truncation times of each observation (or one for every observation), the columns of t, which they replace (#662).

  • init (array_like, optional) – Initial parameter values (baseline parameters followed by the covariate coefficients).

  • fixed (dict, optional) – Parameters to hold fixed, by name.

  • center (bool, optional) – False (the default) fits h_0(x) + beta'Z, the baseline at Z = 0. True fits h_0(x) + beta'(Z - center), the baseline at the covariate means (stored as model.center), with init and fixed read there too. The two are different models: h_0 plus a constant is not a hazard of the baseline’s family (and for the Exponential the positivity bound moves), so, unlike the log-linear families, the additive model is never centred by default.

  • w (array_like or float, optional) – Sampling, propensity or censoring weights, one positive number per row (beside its count n). The fit maximises the weighted (pseudo) likelihood and covariance(), behind every Wald bound, is the robust (sandwich) covariance, as R’s survreg(..., weights = w, robust = TRUE); the likelihood-ratio and bootstrap bounds and the information criteria refuse (see Weighted Data).

Returns:

The fitted model. Warns if the fit ends on the positivity boundary (the hazard nearly zero at an observed failure), and raises if the optimiser cannot reach a finite likelihood.

Return type:

ParametricRegressionModel

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import Weibull, WeibullAH
>>> np.random.seed(1)
>>> Z = np.random.binomial(1, 0.5, 100).reshape(-1, 1)
>>> x = Weibull.random(100, 10, 2) * np.exp(-0.5 * Z[:, 0])
>>> c = np.zeros(100)
>>> model = WeibullAH.fit(x=x, Z=Z, c=c)
>>> model.params.round(3)
array([9.332, 1.851, 0.086])
fit_from_df(df: pd.DataFrame, x_col: str | None = None, Z_cols: str | list[str] | None = None, c_col: str | None = None, n_col: str | None = None, tl_col: str | None = None, tr_col: str | None = None, xl_col: str | None = None, xr_col: str | None = None, formula: str | None = None, init: npt.ArrayLike | None = None, fixed: dict[str, float] | None = None, center: bool = False, w_col: str | None = None, *, unit=None) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit the regression model using a pandas DataFrame as the input.

The names of the covariates are retained on the fitted model so that a DataFrame can later be passed to the prediction methods (sf, ff, df, hf, Hf, random) and the correct columns will be selected automatically.

Parameters:

  • df (pandas.DataFrame) – The dataframe containing the data.

  • x_col (str, optional) – The column name of the observed times. Required unless xl_col and xr_col are given.

  • Z_cols (str or list of str, optional) – The column name(s) of the covariates. Mutually exclusive with formula.

  • c_col (str, optional) – The column name of the censoring indicator.

  • n_col (str, optional) – The column name of the number of observations at each time.

  • tl_col (str, optional) – The column name of the left truncation values.

  • tr_col (str, optional) – The column name of the right truncation values.

  • xl_col (str, optional) – The column names of the left and right ends of each observation’s interval, in place of x_col: the two columns of the (N, 2) x that fit() takes for interval censored data, with c_col giving the censoring of each row as for fit() (#571). Given with x_col, each row is an exact time in x_col or a range in these, the other blank; a row giving both is left out, with a warning.

  • xr_col (str, optional) – The column names of the left and right ends of each observation’s interval, in place of x_col: the two columns of the (N, 2) x that fit() takes for interval censored data, with c_col giving the censoring of each row as for fit() (#571). Given with x_col, each row is an exact time in x_col or a range in these, the other blank; a row giving both is left out, with a warning.

  • formula (str, optional) – A formulaic formula describing the covariates, e.g. "age + sex". Mutually exclusive with Z_cols.

  • init (array_like, optional) – The initial values for the parameters.

  • fixed (dict, optional) – A dictionary of parameters to fix to a specific value.

  • center (bool, optional) – Report the baseline at the covariate means (stored as model.center) instead of at Z = 0; see fit. Not available for an accelerated life model.

  • w_col (str, optional) – The column name of the sampling, propensity or censoring weights, passed to fit as w.

Returns:

The fitted model, with feature_names (and formula) set.

Return type:

ParametricRegressionModel

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> from surpyval import Weibull, WeibullPH
>>> np.random.seed(1)
>>> age = np.random.uniform(20, 60, 100)
>>> weight = np.random.uniform(50, 100, 100)
>>> time = Weibull.random(100, 10, 2) * np.exp(-0.02 * (age - 40))
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({
...     "time": time,
...     "age": age,
...     "weight": weight,
...     "censored": np.zeros(100, dtype=int),
... })
>>> model = WeibullPH.fit_from_df(
...     df, x_col="time", Z_cols=["age", "weight"], c_col="censored"
... )
>>> model.feature_names
['age', 'weight']
>>> model.sf([10, 20], df[["age", "weight"]].head(2)).round(4)
array([0.4757, 0.0024])
fit_tvc(i: npt.ArrayLike, xl: npt.ArrayLike, xr: npt.ArrayLike, c: npt.ArrayLike, Z: npt.ArrayLike, n: npt.ArrayLike | None = None, **kwargs: Any) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit the model to time-varying covariates in start-stop format.

Each row is one observation interval (xl, xr] of subject i on which the covariate row Z is constant; c is 0 (event at xr) only on the interval that ends at the subject’s event and 1 (right-censored) otherwise – surpyval’s censoring convention. The intervals are validated and mapped to left-truncated observations (t = [xl, inf]), then fitted with the ordinary parametric MLE, so the fit is identical to the equivalent non-time-varying data and its log-likelihood is that of sf_tvc / hf along each subject’s covariate path. Extra keyword arguments (init, fixed, center) are passed through to fit.

A subject’s rows must not overlap, it may have at most one event, and that event must be on its last interval; gaps between its intervals (not at risk) and delayed entry (a first xl > 0) are allowed.

A subject’s first row enters at its xl, as any other row does (#952). For a baseline that starts at 0, entering at 0 is no truncation. For one defined below 0 (Normal, Gumbel, Logistic) a first xl of 0 means the subject entered at 0, and the fit conditions on its surviving to 0; give -inf for a subject followed since -inf, its first covariate row holding since then.

Parameters:

  • i (array_like) – Subject identifier of each interval row.

  • xl (array_like) – The open-closed interval (xl, xr] of each row.

  • xr (array_like) – The open-closed interval (xl, xr] of each row.

  • c (array_like) – Status at xr: 0 for the subject’s event, 1 for a right-censored interval end (a covariate change or the end of follow-up).

  • Z (array_like) – The covariate row in force on each interval (a 1-D array is a single covariate).

  • n (array_like, optional) – Count weight of each row. Defaults to 1.

  • **kwargs – Passed to fit (init, fixed, center).

Returns:

The fitted model, with is_tvc set. Evaluate it along a covariate path with sf_tvc / Hf_tvc.

Return type:

ParametricRegressionModel

Examples

Units fail at rate 0.5 until a stress switches on at a random time, and at 0.5 e after it; a unit that outlives its switch contributes two rows:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import WeibullPH
>>> rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
>>> n = 300
>>> switch = rng.uniform(0.3, 1.5, n)
>>> t_low = rng.exponential(2.0, n)
>>> t_high = switch + rng.exponential(2.0 / np.e, n)
>>> T = np.where(t_low > switch, t_high, t_low)
>>> one = T <= switch
>>> i = np.r_[np.arange(n), np.flatnonzero(~one)]
>>> xl = np.r_[np.zeros(n), switch[~one]]
>>> xr = np.r_[np.where(one, T, switch), T[~one]]
>>> c = np.r_[np.where(one, 0, 1), np.zeros((~one).sum(), dtype=int)]
>>> Z = np.r_[np.zeros(n), np.ones((~one).sum())]
>>> model = WeibullPH.fit_tvc(i, xl, xr, c, Z)
>>> model.params.round(3)  # alpha, beta (shape), coef_0
array([2.059, 0.992, 0.995])

The survival of a unit whose stress switches on at time 1:

>>> model.sf_tvc([1.0, 2.0], [[0.0], [1.0]], xl=[0.0, 1.0]).round(4)
array([0.6136, 0.1661])
fit_tvc_from_df(df: pd.DataFrame, i_col: str, xl_col: str, xr_col: str, c_col: str, Z_cols: str | list[str] | None = None, n_col: str | None = None, formula: str | None = None, **kwargs: Any) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit start-stop time-varying-covariate data from a DataFrame.

i_col, xl_col, xr_col, c_col and n_col name the columns passed to fit_tvc() as i, xl, xr, c and n. The covariates are Z_cols, a column name or a list of them, or instead formula, a formulaic formula as in fit_from_df, which codes categorical (e.g. "yes" / "no") columns; give exactly one. The model records feature_names (and the formula and its encoding), so it predicts from a DataFrame with the same design. Other keyword arguments go to fit (init, fixed, center). Returns the fitted ParametricRegressionModel.

Examples

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> from surpyval import WeibullPH
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({
...     "id": [0, 0, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6],
...     "start": [0, 2, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 3, 0, 0],
...     "stop": [2, 5, 3, 1, 4, 6, 3, 7, 2, 8],
...     "c": [1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1],
...     "dose": ["low", "high", "low", "low", "high", "low", "low",
...              "high", "high", "low"],
... })
>>> model = WeibullPH.fit_tvc_from_df(
...     df, "id", "start", "stop", "c", formula="dose"
... )
>>> model.feature_names
['dose[T.low]']
fit_tvc_penalised(i: npt.ArrayLike, xl: npt.ArrayLike, xr: npt.ArrayLike, c: npt.ArrayLike, Z: npt.ArrayLike, n: npt.ArrayLike | None = None, penalizer: float | npt.ArrayLike = 0.1, l1_ratio: float = 0.0, standardise: bool = True, tol: float = 1e-10, w: npt.ArrayLike | float | None = None) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit the model to time-varying covariates in start-stop format (as fit_tvc()) with a ridge, lasso or elastic-net penalty on the coefficients (as fit_penalised).

The rows are validated and fitted as the delayed-entry rows fit_tvc() fits, by fit_penalised’s objective, with N the number of subjects (the distinct i, each weighted by the n of its last row), not of rows, and the covariates standardised over the subjects: each subject’s covariate is its average over its follow-up, each row weighted by its length xr - xl. Splitting a subject’s follow-up into more rows with the same covariates leaves the likelihood unchanged (the cumulative hazard is additive over the rows), and so, with N and the scale per subject, it leaves the fit unchanged too, as for CoxPH.fit_tvc_penalised. The model has no covariance, standard errors, bounds or tests (see fit_penalised).

The parametric additive hazards models (WeibullAH, …) have no penalised fit, with or without time-varying covariates, and refuse: their coefficients are rates, so a penalty on them would depend on the unit of time.

Parameters:

  • i (array_like) – As for fit_tvc().

  • xl (array_like) – As for fit_tvc().

  • xr (array_like) – As for fit_tvc().

  • c (array_like) – As for fit_tvc().

  • Z (array_like) – As for fit_tvc().

  • n (array_like) – As for fit_tvc().

  • penalizer – As for fit_penalised.

  • l1_ratio – As for fit_penalised.

  • standardise – As for fit_penalised.

  • tol – As for fit_penalised.

  • w (None) – Weights are refused here: give them to fit_penalised on rows without time-varying covariates, or to the unpenalised fit_tvc().

Returns:

The fitted model, with is_tvc and penalty set.

Return type:

ParametricRegressionModel

Examples

Units fail at rate 0.5 until a stress switches on at a random time, and at 0.5 e after it; two other covariates do nothing:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import WeibullPH
>>> rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
>>> n = 300
>>> switch = rng.uniform(0.3, 1.5, n)
>>> t_low = rng.exponential(2.0, n)
>>> t_high = switch + rng.exponential(2.0 / np.e, n)
>>> T = np.where(t_low > switch, t_high, t_low)
>>> one = T <= switch
>>> i = np.r_[np.arange(n), np.flatnonzero(~one)]
>>> xl = np.r_[np.zeros(n), switch[~one]]
>>> xr = np.r_[np.where(one, T, switch), T[~one]]
>>> c = np.r_[np.where(one, 0, 1), np.zeros((~one).sum(), dtype=int)]
>>> stress = np.r_[np.zeros(n), np.ones((~one).sum())]
>>> Z = np.column_stack([stress, rng.normal(size=(n, 2))[i]])
>>> model = WeibullPH.fit_tvc_penalised(
...     i, xl, xr, c, Z, penalizer=0.05, l1_ratio=1
... )
>>> model.params.round(3)  # alpha, beta (shape), coefficients
array([1.928, 1.032, 0.895, 0.087, 0.   ])
fit_tvc_timeline(i: npt.ArrayLike, x: npt.ArrayLike, Z: npt.ArrayLike, c: npt.ArrayLike, n: npt.ArrayLike | None = None, **kwargs: Any) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit the model from a covariate timeline (the xicnt-style input).

Each subject’s rows give its covariate history: a value Z takes effect at time x and holds until the subject’s next row, with the terminal event / censoring on the last row’s c (0 event, 1 censored). The timeline is expanded to start-stop intervals and fitted as fit_tvc(), so the fit is identical to the equivalent start-stop data.

Parameters:

  • i (array_like) – Subject identifier of each timeline row.

  • x (array_like) – The time each row’s covariate value takes effect, strictly increasing within a subject: the first is the entry time, the last the event or censoring time.

  • Z (array_like) – The covariate row in force from x; the value on a subject’s last row is ignored.

  • c (array_like) – Status, read from each subject’s last row only (0 event, 1 censored).

  • n (array_like, optional) – Count weight of each subject, read from its last row.

  • **kwargs – Passed to fit (init, fixed, center).

Returns:

The fitted model, with is_tvc set.

Return type:

ParametricRegressionModel

fit_tvc_timeline_from_df(df: pd.DataFrame, i_col: str, x_col: str, Z_cols: str | list[str] | None, c_col: str, n_col: str | None = None, formula: str | None = None, **kwargs: Any) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit a covariate timeline from a DataFrame.

i_col, x_col, c_col and n_col name the columns passed to fit_tvc_timeline() as i, x, c and n. The covariates are Z_cols, a column name or a list of them, or instead (pass Z_cols=None) formula, as for fit_tvc_from_df(); the model records feature_names (and the formula and its encoding). Other keyword arguments go to fit (init, fixed, center). Returns the fitted ParametricRegressionModel.

fit_tvc_timeline_penalised(i: npt.ArrayLike, x: npt.ArrayLike, Z: npt.ArrayLike, c: npt.ArrayLike, n: npt.ArrayLike | None = None, penalizer: float | npt.ArrayLike = 0.1, l1_ratio: float = 0.0, standardise: bool = True, tol: float = 1e-10, w: npt.ArrayLike | float | None = None) → ParametricRegressionModel

fit_tvc_timeline() with a ridge, lasso or elastic-net penalty: the timeline is expanded to start-stop rows and fitted by fit_tvc_penalised(), so it gives the same fit as the equivalent start-stop data.

Parameters:

  • i (array_like) – As for fit_tvc_timeline().

  • x (array_like) – As for fit_tvc_timeline().

  • Z (array_like) – As for fit_tvc_timeline().

  • c (array_like) – As for fit_tvc_timeline().

  • n (array_like) – As for fit_tvc_timeline().

  • penalizer – As for fit_tvc_penalised().

  • l1_ratio – As for fit_tvc_penalised().

  • standardise – As for fit_tvc_penalised().

  • tol – As for fit_tvc_penalised().
