fitter_kind: str = 'additive hazards fitter'

The repr (#614)

hf(x: NDArray | float, Z: NDArray | float, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

Hazard rate \(h_0(x) + \beta' Z\) at x for covariates Z; params are the distribution parameters followed by the coefficients.

name_suffix: str = 'AH'

The end of the public name of a family’s fitter after its distribution’s, for a fitter without a name (WeibullAFT).

neg_ll(data: SurpyvalData, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

The negative log-likelihood of data at params (the distribution parameters followed by the covariate parameters), for every kind of censoring and truncation.

random(size: int, Z: ArrayLike, *params: float, random_state: Any = None) → tuple[NDArray, NDArray]

Draw size samples for each covariate row of Z by numerically inverting the (monotone) cumulative hazard over the baseline’s whole support: on a baseline over the whole real line a share ff(0) of the draws is below 0. A draw outside the model’s support (where the hazard or its integral is negative, so the model is not a distribution) is nan, with one warning (#828).

Returns the draws and a 2-D array of the covariate row each was drawn at, row by row – the same contract as the proportional hazards random. random_state seeds the draw: None (the default) draws from numpy’s global generator, so np.random.seed reproduces it; an int or a numpy.random.Generator gives a stream of its own.

Examples

A Normal baseline puts ff(0) of the mass below 0, and the same share of the draws falls there:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import NormalAH
>>> np.random.seed(0)
>>> x, _ = NormalAH.random(100000, [[1.0]], 10.0, 4.0, 0.05)
>>> round(float(np.mean(x < 0)), 4)
0.0062
>>> NormalAH.ff(np.array([0.0]), np.array([[1.0]]), 10.0, 4.0, 0.05)
array([0.00620967])
sf(x: NDArray | float, Z: NDArray | float, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

Survival function at x for covariates Z, \(R(x \mid Z) = e^{-H(x \mid Z)}\).

params are the distribution parameters followed by the covariate coefficients, in the order of a fitted model’s params. A fitted model’s own sf(x, Z) supplies them.

Spline baseline (Royston-Parmar)

The PH and PO families on a restricted cubic spline baseline in log time, in place of a named distribution: \(\log H(t \mid Z) = s(\log t; \gamma) + \beta' Z\) on the hazard scale. df=1 on the hazard scale is the Weibull PH model. Worked examples are in Regression Modelling with SurPyval.

Pre-built instances, each with three degrees of freedom: RoystonParmarPH (proportional hazards) and RoystonParmarPO (proportional odds).

class surpyval.univariate.regression.royston_parmar_regression.RoystonParmarRegression(df: int = 3, scale: str = 'hazard', knots: ArrayLike | None = None)

Bases: FitterRepr, DataFrameRegressionMixin

Royston-Parmar (flexible parametric) regression: a restricted cubic spline baseline in log time, with df degrees of freedom (df - 1 internal knots), and covariates acting as proportional hazards (scale="hazard") or proportional odds (scale="odds").

The model is

\[\log H(t \mid Z) = s(\log t; \gamma) + \beta' Z\]

on the hazard scale, and \(\operatorname{logit} F(t \mid Z) = s(\log t; \gamma) - \beta' Z\) on the odds scale (the survival odds multiplied by \(e^{\beta' Z}\), as PO). df=1 on the hazard scale is the Weibull proportional hazards model. The fitted model is a ParametricRegressionModel whose baseline parameters are the spline coefficients gamma_j, with every bound (Wald, likelihood ratio and bootstrap, conditional on the knots), summary, fit_from_df and saving.

Parameters:

  • df (int, optional) – Degrees of freedom of the spline: the number of terms beyond the intercept. Default 3. Compare a few by AIC.

  • scale ({"hazard", "odds"}, optional) – How the covariates act. Default "hazard".

  • knots (array_like, optional) – Explicit knots in log time, the boundary knots included, instead of the quantiles of the event times. They are sorted (the spline coefficients follow the sorted knots, as for RoystonParmar.fit) and must be finite and distinct.

Examples

>>> from surpyval import RoystonParmarPH
>>> from surpyval.datasets import load_rossi_static
>>> df = load_rossi_static()
>>> df["censored"] = 1 - df["arrest"]
>>> model = RoystonParmarPH.fit_from_df(
...     df, x_col="week", c_col="censored", Z_cols=["fin", "age", "prio"]
... )
>>> model.params[-3:].round(4)
array([-0.3488, -0.067 ,  0.0974])
family(knots: ArrayLike) → Any

The PH (hazard scale) or PO (odds scale) fitter on the spline baseline with these knots.

fit(x: ArrayLike, Z: ArrayLike, c: ArrayLike | None = None, n: ArrayLike | None = None, t: ArrayLike | None = None, init: ArrayLike | None = None, fixed: dict[str, float] | None = None, center: bool = False, tl: ArrayLike | None = None, tr: ArrayLike | None = None, w: ArrayLike | float | None = None, *, unit=None) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit by maximum likelihood: the knots are placed on the data (or taken from the fitter), then the spline coefficients and the covariate coefficients are fitted together, by the PH or PO family’s fit.

Parameters:

  • x (array_like) – As for WeibullPH.fit: every kind of censoring (x an (N, 2) array for intervals) and left and right truncation.

  • Z (array_like) – As for WeibullPH.fit: every kind of censoring (x an (N, 2) array for intervals) and left and right truncation.

  • c (array_like) – As for WeibullPH.fit: every kind of censoring (x an (N, 2) array for intervals) and left and right truncation.

  • n (array_like) – As for WeibullPH.fit: every kind of censoring (x an (N, 2) array for intervals) and left and right truncation.

  • t (array_like) – As for WeibullPH.fit: every kind of censoring (x an (N, 2) array for intervals) and left and right truncation.

  • tl (array_like) – As for WeibullPH.fit: every kind of censoring (x an (N, 2) array for intervals) and left and right truncation.

  • tr (array_like) – As for WeibullPH.fit: every kind of censoring (x an (N, 2) array for intervals) and left and right truncation.

  • init (array_like, optional) – Initial values: the spline coefficients, then the covariate coefficients. Default the univariate fit’s and zeros.

  • fixed (dict, optional) – Parameters to hold, by name ("gamma_1", a coefficient’s column name or "coef_j").

  • center (bool, optional) – As for WeibullPH.fit.

  • w (array_like or float, optional) – Sampling, propensity or censoring weights, one positive finite weight per row (or one for every row), as for WeibullPH.fit: the weighted estimates with the robust (sandwich) covariance. The knots are placed on the event times counted by n alone, not weighted (so that they do not depend on the weights at all); pass knots to choose them.

Returns:

The fitted model.

Return type:

ParametricRegressionModel

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import RoystonParmarRegression
>>> rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
>>> Z = rng.binomial(1, 0.5, (300, 1))
>>> x = 10 * rng.weibull(1.5, 300) * np.exp(-0.4 * Z[:, 0])
>>> model = RoystonParmarRegression(df=2).fit(x, Z)
>>> model.parameter_names
['gamma_0', 'gamma_1', 'gamma_2', 'coef_0']
fit_from_df(df: pd.DataFrame, x_col: str | None = None, Z_cols: str | list[str] | None = None, c_col: str | None = None, n_col: str | None = None, tl_col: str | None = None, tr_col: str | None = None, xl_col: str | None = None, xr_col: str | None = None, formula: str | None = None, init: npt.ArrayLike | None = None, fixed: dict[str, float] | None = None, center: bool = False, w_col: str | None = None, *, unit=None) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit the regression model using a pandas DataFrame as the input.

The names of the covariates are retained on the fitted model so that a DataFrame can later be passed to the prediction methods (sf, ff, df, hf, Hf, random) and the correct columns will be selected automatically.

Parameters:

  • df (pandas.DataFrame) – The dataframe containing the data.

  • x_col (str, optional) – The column name of the observed times. Required unless xl_col and xr_col are given.

  • Z_cols (str or list of str, optional) – The column name(s) of the covariates. Mutually exclusive with formula.

  • c_col (str, optional) – The column name of the censoring indicator.

  • n_col (str, optional) – The column name of the number of observations at each time.

  • tl_col (str, optional) – The column name of the left truncation values.

  • tr_col (str, optional) – The column name of the right truncation values.

  • xl_col (str, optional) – The column names of the left and right ends of each observation’s interval, in place of x_col: the two columns of the (N, 2) x that fit() takes for interval censored data, with c_col giving the censoring of each row as for fit() (#571). Given with x_col, each row is an exact time in x_col or a range in these, the other blank; a row giving both is left out, with a warning.

  • xr_col (str, optional) – The column names of the left and right ends of each observation’s interval, in place of x_col: the two columns of the (N, 2) x that fit() takes for interval censored data, with c_col giving the censoring of each row as for fit() (#571). Given with x_col, each row is an exact time in x_col or a range in these, the other blank; a row giving both is left out, with a warning.

  • formula (str, optional) – A formulaic formula describing the covariates, e.g. "age + sex". Mutually exclusive with Z_cols.

  • init (array_like, optional) – The initial values for the parameters.

  • fixed (dict, optional) – A dictionary of parameters to fix to a specific value.

  • center (bool, optional) – Report the baseline at the covariate means (stored as model.center) instead of at Z = 0; see fit. Not available for an accelerated life model.

  • w_col (str, optional) – The column name of the sampling, propensity or censoring weights, passed to fit as w.

Returns:

The fitted model, with feature_names (and formula) set.

Return type:

ParametricRegressionModel

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> from surpyval import Weibull, WeibullPH
>>> np.random.seed(1)
>>> age = np.random.uniform(20, 60, 100)
>>> weight = np.random.uniform(50, 100, 100)
>>> time = Weibull.random(100, 10, 2) * np.exp(-0.02 * (age - 40))
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({
...     "time": time,
...     "age": age,
...     "weight": weight,
...     "censored": np.zeros(100, dtype=int),
... })
>>> model = WeibullPH.fit_from_df(
...     df, x_col="time", Z_cols=["age", "weight"], c_col="censored"
... )
>>> model.feature_names
['age', 'weight']
>>> model.sf([10, 20], df[["age", "weight"]].head(2)).round(4)
array([0.4757, 0.0024])
fit_penalised(x: ArrayLike, Z: ArrayLike, c: ArrayLike | None = None, n: ArrayLike | None = None, t: ArrayLike | None = None, penalizer: float | ArrayLike = 0.1, l1_ratio: float = 0.0, standardise: bool = True, tl: ArrayLike | None = None, tr: ArrayLike | None = None, tol: float = 1e-10, w: ArrayLike | float | None = None, *, unit=None) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit with a ridge, lasso or elastic-net penalty on the covariate coefficients (the spline coefficients are not penalised): the knots are placed as fit() places them, then the PH or PO family on the spline baseline is fitted by its fit_penalised (see WeibullPH.fit_penalised for the objective). The model has no covariance, standard errors, bounds or tests.

Parameters:

  • x (array_like) – As for fit().

  • Z (array_like) – As for fit().

  • c (array_like) – As for fit().

  • n (array_like) – As for fit().

  • t (array_like) – As for fit().

  • tl (array_like) – As for fit().

  • tr (array_like) – As for fit().

  • penalizer – As for WeibullPH.fit_penalised (weights w are refused).

  • l1_ratio – As for WeibullPH.fit_penalised (weights w are refused).

  • standardise – As for WeibullPH.fit_penalised (weights w are refused).

  • tol – As for WeibullPH.fit_penalised (weights w are refused).

  • w – As for WeibullPH.fit_penalised (weights w are refused).

The fitted model, with penalty set.

ParametricRegressionModel

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import RoystonParmarPH
>>> rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
>>> Z = rng.normal(size=(300, 3))
>>> x = 10 * rng.weibull(1.5, 300) * np.exp(-0.4 * Z[:, 0])
>>> model = RoystonParmarPH.fit_penalised(
...     x, Z, penalizer=0.05, l1_ratio=1
... )
>>> model.params[-3:].round(3)
array([ 0.572,  0.017, -0.028])
fitter_kind: str = 'flexible parametric (spline) regression fitter'

What the fitter fits, printed after its name.

Accelerated Life (AL)

AL models substitute the life parameter of a distribution with a physics-motivated stress function \(L(Z)\). They are designed for a few discrete, controlled stress levels (e.g. temperature, voltage). Supported distributions, and the parameter the life replaces: Weibull (\(\alpha = L\)), Normal, Gumbel and Logistic (\(\mu = L\)), LogNormal (\(\mu = \ln L\)), Exponential and Gamma (the rate is \(1/L\)).

Factory:

from surpyval import AcceleratedLife, Weibull, life_models
model = AcceleratedLife(Weibull, life_models.Power).fit(x, Z=stress, c=c)
surpyval.univariate.regression.accelerated_life.accelerated_life.AcceleratedLife(distribution: OptimisedFitMixin, life_model: LifeModel) → ParameterSubstitutionFitter

Create an Accelerated Life fitter for the given distribution and life model.

Parameters:

  • distribution (ParametricFitter) – A surpyval parametric distribution (e.g. Weibull, LogNormal).

  • life_model (LifeModel) – A stress-relationship model (e.g. Power, Eyring).

Returns:

A configured fitter with a .fit(x, Z, ...) method.

Return type:

ParameterSubstitutionFitter

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import Weibull
>>> from surpyval import AcceleratedLife
>>> from surpyval.life_models import Power
>>> np.random.seed(1)
>>> stress = np.repeat([20.0, 30.0, 40.0], 40).reshape(-1, 1)
>>> x = Weibull.random(120, 10, 3) * (100.0 / stress[:, 0])
>>> model = AcceleratedLife(Weibull, Power).fit(x, Z=stress)
>>> model.params.round(3)
array([  1.   ,   2.831, 558.686,  -0.828])

The available life models, in surpyval.life_models (until v0.22 importable from surpyval, the exponential one as ExponentialLifeModel), with \(Z\) the stress (\(Z_1, Z_2\) for the two-stress models) and the parameter names as the fitted model reports them:

Life model

\(L(Z)\)

Parameters

Power

\(a Z^{n}\)

a (> 0), n

InversePower

\(1 / (a Z^{n})\)

a (> 0), n

Exponential

\(b\, e^{a / Z}\)

a, b (> 0)

InverseExponential

\(1 / (b\, e^{a / Z})\)

a, b (> 0)

Eyring

\(\frac{1}{Z} e^{-(b - a / Z)}\)

a, b

InverseEyring

\(Z\, e^{c - a / Z}\)

a, c

Linear

\(a + b Z\)

a, b

DualExponential

\(c\, e^{a / Z_1} e^{b / Z_2}\)

a, b, c (> 0)

DualPower

\(c\, Z_1^{m} Z_2^{n}\)

c (> 0), m, n

PowerExponential

\(c\, e^{a / Z_1} Z_2^{n}\)

c (> 0), a, n

GeneralLogLinear

\(c\, e^{\beta_0 Z_0 + \beta_1 Z_1 + \cdots}\), any number of columns

c (> 0), then one coefficient per column (named by the column, or coef_0, coef_1, …)

GeneralLinear

\(a + \beta_0 Z_0 + \beta_1 Z_1 + \cdots\), any number of columns

a, then one coefficient per column (named by the column, or coef_0, coef_1, …)

Custom life models can be created by subclassing LifeModel:

from surpyval import AcceleratedLife
from surpyval.life_models import LifeModel
import autograd.numpy as anp

class MyStressModel(LifeModel):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(
            name="MyStressModel",
            phi_param_map={"a": 0, "b": 1},
            phi_bounds=((None, None), (None, None)),
        )

    def phi(self, Z, *params):
        a, b = params
        return anp.exp(a + b * Z)

    def phi_init(self, life, Z):
        b, a = anp.polyfit(Z.flatten(), anp.log(life), 1)
        return [float(a), float(b)]

model = AcceleratedLife(Weibull, MyStressModel()).fit(x, Z=stress, c=c)

The fit calls a custom model’s phi once for each distinct stress row. If phi also takes a 2-D array of stress rows and gives one life per row, as the built-in models do (MyStressModel does: it is elementwise in Z), set the class attribute phi_takes_rows = True. The fit then finds every row’s life in one call, which matters when the stress is continuous and every row has its own.

class surpyval.univariate.regression.accelerated_life.parameter_substitution.ParameterSubstitutionFitter(kind: str, name: str, distribution: OptimisedFitMixin, life_model: LifeModel, life_parameter: str, baseline: list[str] | str | None = None, param_transform: Callable[[NDArray | float | ArrayBox], NDArray | float | ArrayBox] | None = None, inverse_param_transform: Callable[[NDArray | float | ArrayBox], NDArray | float | ArrayBox] | None = None, life_relation: str = 'L(Z)')

Bases: HazardIdentitiesMixin, RegressionFitter

Accelerated life fitter: the life parameter of a distribution is replaced by a function of the stress, \(L(Z)\), given by a life model (Power, Eyring, …), while the other distribution parameters are shared by every stress level.

Which parameter carries the life, and how, depends on the distribution: \(\alpha = L(Z)\) for Weibull, \(\mu = L(Z)\) for Normal, Gumbel and Logistic, \(\mu = \ln L(Z)\) for LogNormal, and the rate is \(1 / L(Z)\) for Exponential (failure_rate) and Gamma (beta). Create one with AcceleratedLife(distribution, life_model) rather than directly.

df(x: NDArray | float, Z: NDArray | float, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

Density at x for covariates Z, \(f(x \mid Z) = h(x \mid Z) e^{-H(x \mid Z)}\). params as for sf().

Far in the upper tail, where \(H\) is so large that \(e^{-H}\) underflows to 0, the density is 0, also where the hazard itself has overflowed to inf (a large Weibull shape, or a covariate far from 0): it is not inf * 0 (#714).

ff(x: NDArray | float, Z: NDArray | float, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

Failure (CDF) function at x for covariates Z, \(F(x \mid Z) = 1 - e^{-H(x \mid Z)}\). params as for sf().

fit(x: ArrayLike, Z: ArrayLike, c: ArrayLike | None = None, n: ArrayLike | None = None, t: ArrayLike | None = None, init: ArrayLike | None = None, fixed: dict[str, float] | None = None, tl: ArrayLike | None = None, tr: ArrayLike | None = None, w: ArrayLike | float | None = None, *, unit=None) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit the accelerated life model by maximum likelihood.

Parameters:

  • x (array_like) – The observed event times.

  • Z (array_like) – The stress of each observation: a 1-D array for a one-stress life model, or one column per stress (two for DualPower, DualExponential, PowerExponential; any number for GeneralLogLinear, one coefficient each). Designed for a few controlled stress levels: without init the starting point comes from fitting the distribution at each distinct stress level, so at least two levels are needed. Power, InversePower, DualPower and the second (power) stress of PowerExponential need strictly positive stresses; the Arrhenius-type models (Exponential, InverseExponential, the Eyring models, the first stress of DualExponential and PowerExponential) an absolute temperature, in kelvin (a value <= 0 is refused, and a stress below 200 K throughout warns, as degrees Celsius would be). Rows with a missing or infinite stress are dropped, with a warning.

  • c (array_like, optional) – The censoring indicators (0 observed, 1 right, -1 left, 2 interval). Defaults to all observed.

  • n (array_like, optional) – The count of observations at each time. Defaults to 1.

  • t (array_like, optional) – Truncation bounds: an (N, 2) array of the left and right truncation times of each observation.

  • tl (array_like or float, optional) – The left / right truncation times of each observation (or one for every observation), the columns of t, which they replace (#662).

  • tr (array_like or float, optional) – The left / right truncation times of each observation (or one for every observation), the columns of t, which they replace (#662).

  • init (array_like, optional) – Initial parameter values: the distribution parameters (with any value in the life parameter’s slot) followed by the life-model parameters. Where the fit from them does not reach a verified maximum, the default start is tried too and the better kept.

  • fixed (dict, optional) – Parameters to hold fixed, by name (a distribution parameter or a life-model parameter such as "n").

  • w (array_like or float, optional) – Sampling, propensity or censoring weights, one positive number per row (beside its count n). The fit maximises the weighted (pseudo) likelihood and covariance(), behind every Wald bound, is the robust (sandwich) covariance, as R’s survreg(..., weights = w, robust = TRUE); the likelihood-ratio and bootstrap bounds and the information criteria refuse (see Weighted Data).

Returns:

The fitted model. The life parameter’s slot in params and dist_params holds a placeholder value of 1 (it is replaced by the life model at each stress); the life-model parameters are in phi_params. model.data holds the rows sorted by every column (time, censoring, count, truncation, stress), the order the fit runs in, so it is the same whatever order they are given in.

Return type:

ParametricRegressionModel

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import Weibull, AcceleratedLife
>>> from surpyval.life_models import Power
>>> np.random.seed(1)
>>> stress = np.repeat([20.0, 30.0, 40.0], 40)
>>> x = Weibull.random(120, 10, 3) * (100.0 / stress)
>>> model = AcceleratedLife(Weibull, Power).fit(x, Z=stress)
>>> model.params.round(3)
array([  1.   ,   2.831, 558.686,  -0.828])
fit_from_df(df: pd.DataFrame, x_col: str | None = None, Z_cols: str | list[str] | None = None, c_col: str | None = None, n_col: str | None = None, tl_col: str | None = None, tr_col: str | None = None, xl_col: str | None = None, xr_col: str | None = None, formula: str | None = None, init: npt.ArrayLike | None = None, fixed: dict[str, float] | None = None, center: bool = False, w_col: str | None = None, *, unit=None) → ParametricRegressionModel

Fit the regression model using a pandas DataFrame as the input.

The names of the covariates are retained on the fitted model so that a DataFrame can later be passed to the prediction methods (sf, ff, df, hf, Hf, random) and the correct columns will be selected automatically.

Parameters:

  • df (pandas.DataFrame) – The dataframe containing the data.

  • x_col (str, optional) – The column name of the observed times. Required unless xl_col and xr_col are given.

  • Z_cols (str or list of str, optional) – The column name(s) of the covariates. Mutually exclusive with formula.

  • c_col (str, optional) – The column name of the censoring indicator.

  • n_col (str, optional) – The column name of the number of observations at each time.

  • tl_col (str, optional) – The column name of the left truncation values.

  • tr_col (str, optional) – The column name of the right truncation values.

  • xl_col (str, optional) – The column names of the left and right ends of each observation’s interval, in place of x_col: the two columns of the (N, 2) x that fit() takes for interval censored data, with c_col giving the censoring of each row as for fit() (#571). Given with x_col, each row is an exact time in x_col or a range in these, the other blank; a row giving both is left out, with a warning.

  • xr_col (str, optional) – The column names of the left and right ends of each observation’s interval, in place of x_col: the two columns of the (N, 2) x that fit() takes for interval censored data, with c_col giving the censoring of each row as for fit() (#571). Given with x_col, each row is an exact time in x_col or a range in these, the other blank; a row giving both is left out, with a warning.

  • formula (str, optional) – A formulaic formula describing the covariates, e.g. "age + sex". Mutually exclusive with Z_cols.

  • init (array_like, optional) – The initial values for the parameters.

  • fixed (dict, optional) – A dictionary of parameters to fix to a specific value.

  • center (bool, optional) – Report the baseline at the covariate means (stored as model.center) instead of at Z = 0; see fit. Not available for an accelerated life model.

  • w_col (str, optional) – The column name of the sampling, propensity or censoring weights, passed to fit as w.

Returns:

The fitted model, with feature_names (and formula) set.

Return type:

ParametricRegressionModel

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> from surpyval import Weibull, WeibullPH
>>> np.random.seed(1)
>>> age = np.random.uniform(20, 60, 100)
>>> weight = np.random.uniform(50, 100, 100)
>>> time = Weibull.random(100, 10, 2) * np.exp(-0.02 * (age - 40))
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({
...     "time": time,
...     "age": age,
...     "weight": weight,
...     "censored": np.zeros(100, dtype=int),
... })
>>> model = WeibullPH.fit_from_df(
...     df, x_col="time", Z_cols=["age", "weight"], c_col="censored"
... )
>>> model.feature_names
['age', 'weight']
>>> model.sf([10, 20], df[["age", "weight"]].head(2)).round(4)
array([0.4757, 0.0024])
fitter_kind: str = 'accelerated life fitter'

The repr (#614)

name_suffix: str = 'AL'

The end of the public name of a family’s fitter after its distribution’s, for a fitter without a name (WeibullAFT).

neg_ll(data: SurpyvalData, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

The negative log-likelihood of data at params (the distribution parameters followed by the covariate parameters), for every kind of censoring and truncation.

random(size: int, Z: NDArray | float, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox, random_state: Any = None) → tuple[NDArray, NDArray]

Draw size samples at each distinct stress in Z.

Z is a scalar stress, a 1-D array of stresses (one stress variable), or one row per stress for a multi-stress life model. Returns the draws and the stress row each was drawn at. random_state seeds the draw: None (the default) draws from numpy’s global generator, so np.random.seed reproduces it; an int or a numpy.random.Generator gives a stream of its own.

sf(x: NDArray | float, Z: NDArray | float, *params: NDArray | float | ArrayBox) → NDArray | float | ArrayBox

Survival function at x for covariates Z, \(R(x \mid Z) = e^{-H(x \mid Z)}\).

params are the distribution parameters followed by the covariate coefficients, in the order of a fitted model’s params. A fitted model’s own sf(x, Z) supplies them.

class surpyval.univariate.regression.accelerated_life.lifemodel.LifeModel(name: str, phi_param_map: dict[str, int], phi_bounds: tuple[tuple[int | None, int | None], ...])

Bases: FitterRepr, ABC

Base class for the stress-life relationships used by AcceleratedLife: a function \(L(Z)\) giving the life parameter of a distribution at stress \(Z\).

A subclass passes its name, a phi_param_map from parameter name to position, and phi_bounds (one (lower, upper) pair per parameter, None for unbounded) to this constructor, and implements phi() and phi_init(). The built-in life models are instances of subclasses: Power, InversePower, Eyring, InverseEyring, ExponentialLifeModel, InverseExponential, Linear, DualExponential, DualPower, PowerExponential and GeneralLogLinear.

A life model whose parameters depend on the number of stress columns (GeneralLogLinear, one coefficient per column) sets n_stresses = None and overrides resolve(), which the fit calls with the number of columns of Z to get the model with a fixed phi_param_map and phi_bounds.

Examples

Power is one, with \(L(Z) = a Z^n\):

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval.life_models import LifeModel, Power
>>> isinstance(Power, LifeModel)
True
>>> Power.phi_param_map
{'a': 0, 'n': 1}
>>> Power.phi(np.array([1.0, 2.0, 4.0]), 1000.0, -2.0)
array([1000.  ,  250.  ,   62.5])
activation_parameter: tuple[str, float] | None = None

For a thermally activated model, the parameter that is the activation energy over Boltzmann’s constant, E_a / k_B in kelvin, and its sign (-1 where the parameter is -E_a / k_B, as in the models written for the rate); None for the others. ParametricRegressionModel.activation_energy reads it.

property canonical_name: str

its name, except for an alias (Arrhenius gives "Exponential"). The package identifies a life model by it.

Examples

>>> from surpyval import life_models
>>> life_models.Arrhenius.canonical_name
'Exponential'
Type:

The life model’s canonical name

coefficient_columns() → dict[str, int]

The life-model parameters that are each the coefficient of one column of Z as it is (the log-life linear in that column), by name, with the column’s number: the fit searches and judges each in its covariate’s units (coefficient_floor, #612). None for a life model of a transformed stress (log s, 1 / s); one per column for GeneralLogLinear.

Examples

>>> from surpyval.life_models import GeneralLogLinear, Power
>>> Power.coefficient_columns()
{}
>>> GeneralLogLinear.resolve(2).coefficient_columns()
{'coef_0': 0, 'coef_1': 1}
fitter_kind: str = 'life model'

Power: life model (#614)

Type:

The repr

kelvin_stress_columns: tuple[int, ...] = ()

Stress columns read as an absolute temperature, in kelvin (the Arrhenius-type models): the fit refuses a value <= 0 there, naming kelvin, and warns when every value is below KELVIN_WARNING_BELOW (a temperature typed in degrees Celsius, #654).

log_life(Z: ndarray, *params: float) → ndarray

The log of the life, \(\ln L(Z)\), with each of log_scale_parameters given as its log: for a life model whose log-life is linear in them (PowerExponential’s \(\ln c + a / U + n \ln V\)), which its phi() is the exponent of. The fit computes the life from it, on the log scale it searches those parameters on, so that the life stays finite where a factor alone would not (\(e^{a/U}\) overflowing, or c underflowing, where their product is an ordinary life, #634). Only for a model with log_scale_parameters.

log_scale_parameters: tuple[str, ...] = ()

The parameters that multiply the life, a positive factor (c of PowerExponential, a of Power): log_life() takes each as its log, and the fit searches it on the log scale over its whole range (#634).

n_stresses: int | None = 1

The number of stress columns Z has (None when it depends on the data, as for GeneralLogLinear). Lets a single 1-D row [T, V] be read as one two-stress row rather than two stresses.

named(names: Sequence[str]) → LifeModel

This life model with the coefficients of coefficient_columns() named names, in column order (a fit’s covariate columns, #614): GeneralLogLinear’s are coef_0, coef_1, … unless named. A model without such coefficients returns itself.

Examples

>>> from surpyval.life_models import GeneralLogLinear, Power
>>> Power.named(["temp"]) is Power
True
>>> GeneralLogLinear.resolve(2).named(["temp", "volt"]).phi_param_map
{'c': 0, 'temp': 1, 'volt': 2}
abstractmethod phi(Z: ndarray, *params: float) → ndarray

The life \(L(Z)\) at stress Z for the life-model parameters params. Must be written with autograd.numpy so the fit can differentiate it.

abstractmethod phi_init(life: float, Z: ndarray) → list[float]

Starting values for the life-model parameters, given the life estimated separately at each distinct stress level (life, one value per row of Z). Typically a least-squares fit of the linearised relationship.

phi_takes_rows: bool = False

Whether phi() takes a 2-D array of stress rows and gives one life per row, as the built-in models do; the fit then finds every row’s life in one call. False (the default, for a custom model written for a single stress) calls it once per distinct stress.

positive_stress_columns: tuple[int, ...] = ()

the life model takes a power or logarithm of them (Z**n, log Z), or reads them as an absolute temperature.

Type:

Stress columns that must be strictly positive

resolve(n_stresses: int) → LifeModel

The life model for n_stresses stress columns. A model with a fixed number of parameters is the same for any number, and returns itself (a wrong number of columns is refused by the fit); GeneralLogLinear returns the model with one coefficient per column.

Examples

>>> from surpyval.life_models import GeneralLogLinear, Power
>>> Power.resolve(1) is Power
True
>>> GeneralLogLinear.resolve(2).phi_param_map
{'c': 0, 'coef_0': 1, 'coef_1': 2}
warns_below_kelvin: bool = True

Whether the fit warns when every value of a kelvin column is below KELVIN_WARNING_BELOW; Eyring, also used for a non-thermal stress, does not.

Time-varying covariate schedules

A StepSchedule describes a piecewise-constant covariate path Z(t) for sf_tvc / Hf_tvc evaluation. Build one structurally (from_changepoints / from_intervals / cyclic / constant) or from a step-valued expression string in t (from_expression); see Time-varying covariates across families for worked examples. StepValuedError is raised when an expression is not provably step-valued.

class surpyval.univariate.regression.tvc_schedule.StepSchedule(edges: ArrayLike, Z: ArrayLike, period: float | None = None)

Bases: object

A piecewise-constant covariate path Z(t) for time-varying-covariate evaluation.

The canonical form is a set of edges (segment boundaries) and a Z matrix with one covariate row per segment: segment i covers [edges[i], edges[i + 1]) and carries covariate Z[i]. Beyond the last edge the final segment’s covariate is held constant (or, when period is set, the pattern repeats). Z is always two-dimensional, so a schedule is multivariate for free (a single covariate is p = 1).

Construct one with a class method rather than the raw constructor:

  • constant() – a fixed covariate (reduces to the ordinary sf);

  • from_changepoints() – (time, value) pairs, the value taking effect at each time;

  • from_intervals() – explicit (xl, xr] interval rows, matching the fit_tvc start-stop layout;

  • cyclic() – a within-period pattern repeated to a horizon;

  • from_expression() – a step-valued expression string in t.

All the family math needs is segments().

Examples

A covariate that switches from 0 to 1 at time 50, used to predict survival from a fitted proportional hazards model:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import StepSchedule, WeibullPH
>>> schedule = StepSchedule.from_changepoints([0, 50], [0.0, 1.0])
>>> schedule.edges
array([ 0., 50., inf])
>>> rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
>>> Z = rng.binomial(1, 0.5, (100, 1)).astype(float)
>>> x = 100 * rng.weibull(2, 100) * np.exp(-0.25 * Z[:, 0])
>>> model = WeibullPH.fit(x, Z)
>>> model.sf_tvc([40, 80, 120], schedule).round(4)
array([0.9015, 0.4598, 0.1128])

Before time 50 that is the survival at Z = 0; after it, the hazard of Z = 1 applies:

>>> model.sf(np.array([40, 80, 120]), [0.0]).round(4)
array([0.9015, 0.6008, 0.2746])
classmethod constant(Z: ArrayLike) → StepSchedule

A constant covariate Z over all time, from -inf (#952). Evaluating a model on it is identical to model.sf(x, Z).

classmethod cyclic(pattern_times: ArrayLike, pattern_values: ArrayLike, period: float) → StepSchedule

A within-period covariate pattern repeated indefinitely.

pattern_times are the change-points within one period (starting at 0 and all < period); pattern_values the covariate on each. The pattern repeats every period and is materialised up to whatever horizon segments() is asked for – for duty cycles.

Parameters:

  • pattern_times (array_like, shape (m,)) – Change-points within one period, 0 <= t < period, strictly increasing (the first should be 0).

  • pattern_values (array_like, shape (m,) or (m, p)) – The covariate row active from each within-period change-point.

  • period (float) – The repetition period.

classmethod from_changepoints(times: ArrayLike, values: ArrayLike) → StepSchedule

Build a schedule from (time, value) change-points.

values[i] is the covariate row in effect from times[i] until the next change-point; the last value is held to the horizon. times must be strictly increasing; times[0] is the path’s start, start, and may be -inf (the first value held since -inf). A path must cover every time a model’s answer depends on, and one starting later is refused, as nothing says what the covariate was before it: from 0 for a baseline that starts at 0 (the part before 0 is ignored); from -inf for a proportional hazards or proportional odds model on a baseline over the whole real line (Normal, Gumbel, Logistic), and from 0, and any earlier time asked about, for accelerated failure time and additive hazards, which measure the covariate’s effect from 0 (#952). On a record it must start at or before the start of the item’s observation.

Parameters:

  • times (array_like, shape (m,)) – The instants at which the covariate takes each value.

  • values (array_like, shape (m,) or (m, p)) – The covariate row active from each time.

classmethod from_expression(expr: str | list[str], horizon: float, resolution: float = 1.0, t0: float = 0.0) → StepSchedule

Build a schedule from a step-valued expression string (or list of strings) in the free variable t.

The expression is parsed and proved piecewise-constant before it is ever evaluated: t may reach the value only through a quantizer (floor, ceil, //) or a comparison. A continuously-varying expression (0.3 + 1e-4 * t, sin(t)) raises StepValuedError. The allowed syntax means what it does in Python: and / or return an operand, and keyword arguments (round(t / 10, ndigits=1)) are passed on; one a function cannot take raises ValueError.

The (guaranteed stepped) expression is then materialised by sampling on a grid of spacing resolution over [t0, horizon] and coalescing runs of equal value into segments, so resolution must be no coarser than the narrowest step (e.g. 1 hour for an 8-on/16-off duty cycle).

Parameters:

  • expr (str or list of str) – A scalar covariate (p = 1) or, for a multivariate covariate, one expression per covariate.

  • horizon (float) – Materialise the schedule out to this time.

  • resolution (float, optional) – Grid spacing for sampling. Default 1.0.

  • t0 (float, optional) – Start of the path. Default 0.0.

Examples

>>> duty = StepSchedule.from_expression(
...     "0.9 if t % 24 < 8 else 0.3", 96
... )
>>> duty.edges[:4], duty.Z[:4].ravel()
(array([ 0.,  8., 24., 32.]), array([0.9, 0.3, 0.9, 0.3]))
>>> StepSchedule.from_expression("0.3 * 2 ** floor(t / 1000)", 1000)
StepSchedule.from_changepoints([0.0, 1000.0], [[0.3], [0.6]])
classmethod from_intervals(xl: ArrayLike, xr: ArrayLike, Z: ArrayLike) → StepSchedule

Build a schedule from explicit (xl, xr] interval rows – the same layout fit_tvc consumes.

The intervals must be contiguous (each xr equals the next xl); the covariate beyond the final xr is held constant. Rows may be given in any order and are sorted by xl.

property p: int

Number of covariates (columns of Z).

segments(t_max: float) → tuple[NDArray, NDArray, NDArray]

Materialise the schedule up to t_max into concrete step segments.

Returns (starts, ends, Z) with one row per segment, contiguous and covering [edges[0], t_max]. The final segment (or, for a cyclic schedule, every repetition) is clipped so ends[-1] == t_max. This is the sole interface the family cumulative-hazard math consumes.

Parameters:

t_max (float) – The horizon to materialise to (typically the largest query time).

property start: float

The time the schedule starts, its first edge (-inf for one held since -inf): it gives no value before it.

class surpyval.univariate.regression.tvc_schedule.StepValuedError

Bases: ValueError

Raised when an expression covariate schedule is not provably step-valued.

The message points at the sub-expression through which t reaches the output continuously (e.g. a bare t or sin(t)), so the offending term can be quantized (floor(t / dt)) or replaced.

Examples

>>> from surpyval import StepSchedule, StepValuedError
>>> try:
...     StepSchedule.from_expression("2 * t", 10)
... except StepValuedError as error:
...     print(error)
expression '2 * t' is not step-valued: t reaches the value
continuously. Quantize it (e.g. floor(t / dt)) or use a comparison so
the covariate stays piecewise-constant.

Quantized, the same growth is accepted:

>>> StepSchedule.from_expression("2 * floor(t / 5)", 10)
StepSchedule.from_changepoints([0.0, 5.0, 10.0], [[0.0], [2.0], [4.0]])

A CovariatePath describes a continuously varying covariate path: straight lines between points (from_points, a repeated time being a jump) or a vectorised function of time (from_callable), either optionally periodic. sf_tvc / Hf_tvc integrate the model’s hazard along it to a relative error of about 1e-10 (cb_tvc and mean_tvc build on them), and Cox sums its baseline jumps along it exactly. It is a known, external path. A fitted model is evaluated along it, and item records whose time_varying_covariates are paths are fitted on them, each path cut into steps (to_steps) that are halved until the fit stops moving. See Continuously varying covariates and Fitting on a continuous path.

class surpyval.univariate.regression.tvc_path.CovariatePath(evaluate: Callable[[NDArray, bool], NDArray], p: int, knots: NDArray, period: float | None, kind: str)

Bases: object

A continuously varying covariate path Z(t): for evaluating a model along it, model.sf_tvc(x, path) and model.Hf_tvc(x, path), and, as the time_varying_covariates of item records, for fitting one on it.

Build one with a class method rather than the raw constructor:

  • from_points() – straight lines between (time, value) points, a repeated time being a jump (ramps, ramp-hold-step test profiles, sampled measurements);

  • from_callable() – a vectorised function of time (a thermal cycle, a fitted trend).

Either can repeat with a period. Calling the path, path(t), returns its values, one row per time, shape (n, p); at a jump the value at the jump time is the one before it (the left value), as for a covariate recorded in (start, stop] rows.

Where StepSchedule describes a piecewise-constant path, whose survival is an exact sum over the segments, a CovariatePath is integrated by adaptive quadrature to a relative accuracy of about 1e-10 on the cumulative hazard (exactly, with no quadrature, for Cox). The path is measured from time 0, so for a prediction it must start at or before 0 (start), and on a baseline defined below 0 at or before every time the answer depends on, to -inf for proportional hazards and odds, where it is integrated below 0 too (#957); after its last time the last value applies. Survival given an age (given=) under proportional hazards or odds, additive hazards or Cox depends on the path from that age on only, so it need only start by then (#962).

The path must be external – known in advance and not driven by the unit’s own failure process (a planned load, a test profile, ambient conditions) – for the survival along it to be a probability. A model is fitted to steps (fit_tvc): items whose time_varying_covariates are a CovariatePath are fitted on the path cut into steps (to_steps()), halved until no estimate moves by more than 1% of its standard error; the model’s path_steps says what that took.

Examples

A stress ramped from 0 to 1 over 50 hours, then stepped down to 0.6:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import CovariatePath
>>> ramp = CovariatePath.from_points([0, 50, 50], [0.0, 1.0, 0.6])
>>> ramp
CovariatePath(points, 2 knot(s), p=1)
>>> ramp([25, 50, 80]).ravel()
array([0.5, 1. , 0.6])

The survival of a fitted proportional hazards model along the ramp lies between those at the two ends of the stress range:

>>> from surpyval import WeibullPH
>>> rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
>>> Z = rng.uniform(0, 1, (200, 1))
>>> x = 100 * rng.weibull(2, 200) * np.exp(-0.5 * Z[:, 0])
>>> model = WeibullPH.fit(x, Z)
>>> model.sf_tvc([40, 80], ramp).round(4)
array([0.771 , 0.3106])
>>> model.sf(np.array([40, 80]), [0.0]).round(4)
array([0.885, 0.613])
>>> model.sf(np.array([40, 80]), [1.0]).round(4)
array([0.622 , 0.1493])
__call__(t: ArrayLike) → NDArray

The covariate at the times t: one row per time, shape (n, p). A missing (NaN) time gives a row of NaN.

Examples

>>> from surpyval import CovariatePath
>>> CovariatePath.from_points([0, 10], [[0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 3.0]])([5])
array([[0.5, 2. ]])
breakpoints(t_max: float) → NDArray

The path’s knots (for from_points()) or declared breakpoints (for from_callable()) in (0, t_max), repeated every period for a periodic path, with the period boundaries.

Examples

>>> from surpyval import CovariatePath
>>> path = CovariatePath.from_points([0, 5], [0.0, 1.0], period=8)
>>> path.breakpoints(20)
array([ 5.,  8., 13., 16.])
classmethod from_callable(func: Callable[[NDArray], Any], p: int = 1, breakpoints: ArrayLike | None = None, period: float | None = None) → CovariatePath

A path given by a vectorised function of time.

func takes a one-dimensional array of n times and returns the covariate at each, shape (n,) (for one covariate) or (n, p); a scalar is taken as constant. Its values must be finite. The quadrature finds kinks and jumps by refining around them, but list any you know in breakpoints so the panels line up with them: it is faster and certain. With period the path at t is func(t mod period), so func need only describe one period, and breakpoints lie in [0, period].

Parameters:

  • func (callable) – func(t) -> values for an array t.

  • p (int, optional) – Number of covariates. Default 1.

  • breakpoints (array_like, optional) – Times at which func has a kink or a jump.

  • period (float, optional) – The repetition period, if the path repeats.

Examples

A daily thermal cycle between 0 and 1:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import CovariatePath
>>> cycle = CovariatePath.from_callable(
...     lambda t: 0.5 - 0.5 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * t / 24), period=24)
>>> cycle([0, 12, 36]).ravel().round(6)
array([0., 1., 1.])

A stress that climbs until 100 hours and is then held:

>>> climb = CovariatePath.from_callable(
...     lambda t: np.sqrt(np.minimum(t, 100.0)) / 10,
...     breakpoints=[100.0])
>>> climb([25, 100, 400]).ravel()
array([0.5, 1. , 1. ])
classmethod from_points(times: ArrayLike, values: ArrayLike, period: float | None = None) → CovariatePath

A piecewise-linear path through (time, value) points.

Between two points the covariate changes linearly; a time given twice is a jump from the first value to the second. Before the first point the path has no value (it starts there, start), and after the last point the last value applies. With period the pattern repeats: the path at t is the pattern at t mod period, so times must start at 0 and lie in [0, period] (a sawtooth or a thermal cycle).

Parameters:

  • times (array_like, shape (m,)) – The times of the points, non-decreasing; a time may appear at most twice (the two sides of a jump).

  • values (array_like, shape (m,) or (m, p)) – The covariate row at each point.

  • period (float, optional) – The repetition period, if the pattern repeats.

Examples

A load ramped up over 10 hours, held, then dropped at 30:

>>> from surpyval import CovariatePath
>>> path = CovariatePath.from_points([0, 10, 30, 30],
...                                  [0.0, 2.0, 2.0, 0.5])
>>> path([5, 20, 30, 40]).ravel()
array([1. , 2. , 2. , 0.5])

A sawtooth, rising from 0 to 1 every 24 hours:

>>> saw = CovariatePath.from_points([0, 24], [0.0, 1.0], period=24)
>>> saw([6, 30, 54]).ravel()
array([0.25, 0.25, 0.25])
property p: int

Number of covariates (columns of the path’s values).

property start: float

its first point (for from_points() without a period), else -inf, as a function of time, or a pattern that repeats, has a value at every time. It gives no value before it.

Type:

The time the path starts

to_steps(t_max: float, steps: int = 8, start: float | None = None) → Any

The path up to t_max as a step schedule, for fitting a model on it: a model is fitted to steps (fit_tvc), so a continuous path is cut into steps fine enough that the fit no longer depends on them.

Each stretch of the path between two of its breakpoints (the points of from_points(), the declared breakpoints of from_callable(), the ends of each period) is cut into steps steps of equal width, each holding the path’s value at its midpoint. A stretch on which the path takes one value (at every midpoint, and near both ends) is one step, and neighbouring steps of one value are merged, so a path that is flat, or made of steps, comes back as exactly those steps whatever steps is. For a straight ramp the midpoint value is the step’s average, and in general the error of a model’s cumulative hazard along the steps falls with the square of their width.

Parameters:

  • t_max (float) – The age to step the path up to. The last step’s value holds beyond it.

  • steps (int, optional) – The steps in each stretch between breakpoints. Default 8.

  • start (float, optional) – The age the schedule starts at. Default the path’s own start, or 0 for a path with a value at every time (a function, a repeating pattern).

Returns:

The steps, starting at start.

Return type:

StepSchedule

Examples

A ramp from 0 to 1 over 10 hours, then held, as four steps and the hold:

>>> from surpyval import CovariatePath
>>> ramp = CovariatePath.from_points([0, 10], [0.0, 1.0])
>>> stepped = ramp.to_steps(25, steps=4)
>>> stepped.edges
array([ 0. ,  2.5,  5. ,  7.5, 10. ,  inf])
>>> stepped.Z.ravel()
array([0.125, 0.375, 0.625, 0.875, 1.   ])

The fitted model

Every parametric regression fit returns a ParametricRegressionModel carrying the fitted distribution and covariate parameters together with prediction, plotting and serialisation methods.

class surpyval.univariate.regression.parametric_regression_model.ParametricRegressionModel

Bases: AcceleratedLifeAnalysisMixin, ParameterBoundsMixin, AtCovariatesMixin, PenalisedModelMixin, ConditionalSurvivalMixin, RestrictedMeanMixin, PartialEffectsMixin, TVCEvaluationMixin, InferenceMixin, ConcordanceMixin, InformationCriteriaMixin, DiagnoseMixin, SerialisableMixin, PredictsRecordsMixin

The fitted model returned by every parametric regression fitter: the proportional hazards (WeibullPH, PH(dist)), accelerated failure time (AFT), proportional odds (PO), parametric additive hazards (AH) and accelerated life (AcceleratedLife) families.

params holds the distribution parameters followed by the covariate coefficients (dist_params and phi_params split them), named in order by parameter_names. In an accelerated life model the life parameter (life_parameter, e.g. the Weibull’s alpha) is not estimated: the life model gives it at each stress, and its slot in params holds a placeholder 1, which the printed model does not show as a value. The survival functions take the covariates as a second argument, sf(x, Z); sf_tvc / Hf_tvc evaluate them along a time-varying covariate path. The model also provides parameter standard errors and confidence bounds, information criteria, plotting and serialisation.

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import Weibull, WeibullPH
>>> np.random.seed(1)
>>> Z = np.random.binomial(1, 0.5, 100).reshape(-1, 1)
>>> x = Weibull.random(100, 10, 2) * np.exp(-0.5 * Z[:, 0])
>>> model = WeibullPH.fit(x, Z)
>>> model.params.round(3)
array([9.629, 1.751, 0.829])
>>> model.sf(5, [[0], [1]]).round(4)
array([0.728 , 0.4833])
Hf(x: npt.ArrayLike, Z: npt.ArrayLike | pd.DataFrame, *, grid: bool = False) → npt.NDArray

The cumulative hazard function for a distribution using the parameters found in the .params attribute.

Parameters:

  • x (array like or scalar) – The values of the random variables at which the cumulative hazard function will be calculated

  • Z (array like or DataFrame) – The covariates: one row per value of x (or a single row, broadcast to every x), in the column order used in the fit. A model fitted with fit_from_df also accepts a DataFrame with the named (or formula) columns. Other row counts are refused.

  • grid (bool, optional) – True evaluates every x for every row of Z (a curve per subject, lifelines’ predict_survival_function), with shape (len(Z),) + x.shape, row i for row i of Z (#488). Default False: rows and times paired.

Returns:

Hf – The scalar value of the cumulative hazard function of the distribution if a scalar was passed. If an array like object was passed then a numpy array is returned with the value of the cumulative hazard function at each corresponding value in the input array.

Return type:

scalar or numpy array

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import Weibull, WeibullPH
>>> np.random.seed(1)
>>> Z = np.random.binomial(1, 0.5, 100).reshape(-1, 1)
>>> x = Weibull.random(100, 10, 2) * np.exp(-0.5 * Z[:, 0])
>>> model = WeibullPH.fit(x, Z)
>>> model.Hf([1, 2, 3], [[0], [0], [1]]).round(4)
array([0.0189, 0.0638, 0.2972])
Hf_tvc(x: ArrayLike, Z: ArrayLike | Any, xl: ArrayLike | None = None) → NDArray

Cumulative hazard for a covariate following a path Z(t): a step schedule, or a continuously varying path.

For the proportional-hazards, additive-hazards and proportional-odds families the hazard at time \(t\) depends only on \(t\) and the covariate value at \(t\), so along a piecewise constant path the cumulative hazard is exactly the sum of the per-segment increments of the constant-covariate cumulative hazard

\[H\bigl(x \mid Z(\cdot)\bigr) = \sum_{\text{seg } (a, b]} \bigl[\,H(b, z) - H(a, z)\,\bigr] .\]

For proportional odds, with \(\phi = e^{\beta' z}\) multiplying the survival odds, the hazard is \(h(t \mid z) = h_0(t) / (F_0(t) + \phi S_0(t))\) and its integral at constant \(z\) is \(H(t, z) = H_0(t) - \ln\phi + \ln(F_0(t) + \phi S_0(t)) = -\ln S(t \mid z)\), so each segment contributes \(\ln[S(a \mid z) / S(b \mid z)]\). On entering a segment the hazard switches to the new covariate’s PO hazard; the survival does not jump to the new covariate’s PO curve. The first segment is held back to the bottom of the baseline’s support (for a baseline defined below zero, such as Logistic, the value in force at time zero is taken to apply before it too), so the result is the unconditional survival.

For accelerated failure time the covariate rescales time, so the path accumulates an accelerated age \(\psi(x) = \sum_{\text{seg}} e^{\beta' z}\,(b - a)\) and the cumulative hazard is the baseline evaluated there, \(H(x \mid Z(\cdot)) = H_0(\psi(x))\). An accelerated life model whose life parameter scales time (Weibull alpha, the Exponential and Gamma rates, LogNormal’s exp(mu)) does the same with the rate \(1 / L(z)\) and the distribution at unit life, Nelson’s cumulative exposure; one whose life parameter is a location (Normal, Gumbel, Logistic) raises NotImplementedError. Either way a single constant segment reduces exactly to Hf(x, Z).

Along a CovariatePath, a covariate that changes continuously, the same hazards are integrated: \(H(x) = \int_0^x h(u \mid Z(u))\, du\), and for accelerated failure time \(\psi(x) = \int_0^x e^{\beta' Z(u)}\, du\) (Nelson’s cumulative exposure). For proportional odds the hazard is that of the current covariate, \(h_0(t) / (F_0(t) + \phi(Z(t)) S_0(t))\): the limit of the step sum above, and the model fit_tvc fits. The integral is by adaptive Gauss-Kronrod quadrature to a relative error of about 1e-10; where that is not reached, one RuntimeWarning says at how many query times. The type of Z picks the method: a StepSchedule is always summed exactly.

The path is measured from time zero: a schedule or path starting after zero is refused (nothing says what the covariate was before it), and the part of one before zero is ignored (the value in force at zero applies from there). Any time is a valid query, zero and below included: a constant path gives Hf(x, Z) there too.

Parameters:

  • x (array_like) – Times at which to evaluate the cumulative hazard.

  • Z (StepSchedule, CovariatePath or array_like) – The covariate path – a StepSchedule, a CovariatePath, or an array of per-segment covariate rows (with xl giving the segment start times).

  • xl (array_like, optional) – Segment start times, required only when Z is an array.

Returns:

The cumulative hazard at each x.

Return type:

ndarray

Examples

An exponential proportional hazards model along a stress ramp Z(t) = 0.1 t, whose cumulative hazard is \(\lambda (e^{0.1 \beta t} - 1) / (0.1 \beta)\):

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import CovariatePath, ExponentialPH
>>> rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
>>> Z = rng.uniform(0, 2, (300, 1))
>>> x = rng.exponential(10 * np.exp(-0.7 * Z[:, 0]))
>>> model = ExponentialPH.fit(x, Z)
>>> lam, beta = model.params
>>> ramp = CovariatePath.from_points([0, 10], [0.0, 1.0])
>>> t = np.array([2.0, 5.0, 10.0])
>>> H = model.Hf_tvc(t, ramp)
>>> exact = lam * np.expm1(0.1 * beta * t) / (0.1 * beta)
>>> bool(np.allclose(H, exact, rtol=1e-12, atol=0))
True
activation_energy(alpha_ci: float = 0.05, method: str = 'wald', n_boot: int = 200, random_state: Any = None) → dict

The activation energy \(E_a\) of a thermally activated life model (Arrhenius, life_models.Arrhenius or Exponential; Eyring; and their inverses), in electronvolts, with its two-sided 1 - alpha_ci interval.

The life model’s parameter is \(E_a / k_B\) in kelvin (the temperatures in kelvin); \(E_a\) is it times Boltzmann’s constant, \(k_B = 8.617333262\times 10^{-5}\) eV/K (exact in the SI). The interval is the parameter’s param_cb() by method ("wald", "lr" or "bootstrap"), scaled the same way.

Parameters:

  • alpha_ci (float, optional) – The significance level of the interval, by default 0.05.

  • method (str, optional) – "wald" (the default), "lr" or "bootstrap", as for param_cb().

  • n_boot (int, optional) – The refits of a bootstrap, by default 200.

  • random_state (optional) – The seed of a bootstrap.

Returns:

"activation_energy" (eV), "lower" and "upper" (eV), "kelvin" (\(E_a / k_B\), K, with "kelvin_lower" and "kelvin_upper"), "parameter" (the life model’s parameter it comes from), "alpha_ci" and "method".

Return type:

dict

Raises:

ValueError – If the model is not an accelerated life model, or its life model is not thermally activated.

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import surpyval as sp
>>> from surpyval import life_models
>>> rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
>>> T = np.repeat([358.15, 378.15, 398.15], 20)
>>> life = 1e-6 * np.exp(0.7 / 8.617333262e-5 / T)
>>> x = life * rng.weibull(2.0, T.size)
>>> model = sp.AcceleratedLife(sp.Weibull, life_models.Arrhenius)
>>> model = model.fit(x, Z=T)
>>> energy = model.activation_energy()
>>> round(energy["activation_energy"], 3), round(energy["kelvin"])
(0.618, 7169)
>>> round(energy["lower"], 3), round(energy["upper"], 3)
(0.529, 0.707)
aic() → float

The Aikake Information Criterion (AIC) for the model, if it was fit with the fit() method. Not available if fit with the from_params() method.

Returns:

aic – The AIC of the model

Return type:

float

Examples

>>> from surpyval import Weibull
>>> import numpy as np
>>> np.random.seed(1)
>>> x = Weibull.random(100, 10, 3)
>>> model = Weibull.fit(x)
>>> model.aic()
529.0537128478127
aic_c() → float

The Corrected Aikake Information Criterion (AIC) for the model, if it was fit with the fit() method. Not available if fit with the from_params() method.

Returns:

aic_c – The Corrected AIC of the model

Return type:

float

Examples

>>> from surpyval import Weibull
>>> import numpy as np
>>> np.random.seed(1)
>>> x = Weibull.random(100, 10, 3)
>>> model = Weibull.fit(x)
>>> model.aic_c()
529.1774241880189

Notes

The correction \((2k^2 + 2k)/(N - k - 1)\) uses the same sample size \(N\) as bic(): the number of observed failures (exact, left- or interval-censored, weighted by their counts), or the number of units when there is none. Right-censored units do not add to it. The correction only exists for \(N > k + 1\); otherwise the corrected criterion is undefined and nan is returned (the formula gave inf at \(N = k + 1\), and a value below aic() for smaller \(N\), which would have won a comparison).

property aliased: NDArray

The columns of Z whose coefficients the data cannot determine (#476): a constant column where the family has an intercept, or a linear combination of the others. Their coefficients are nan in params (R’s NA), as are their standard errors, and predictions take them as 0. For an accelerated-life model, whose parameters are not one per column, they are positions in phi_params: a stress effect the data cannot determine (#503), such as the second of two equal stress columns of DualPower.

at(Z: Any) → LifeAtCovariates

The life of a unit with the covariates Z, as a plain life model: an object whose sf, ff, df, hf, Hf, qf, random and mean take times (or probabilities) only, each the model’s own at Z (at(Z).sf(x) is sf(x, Z)). Hand it to code that expects a univariate model.

Parameters:

Z (array like or DataFrame) – One covariate row (a scalar for a one-covariate model; a one-row DataFrame for a model fitted with fit_from_df). Several rows are refused: call it once per row.

Returns:

A view on this model at Z.

Return type:

LifeAtCovariates

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import Weibull, WeibullPH
>>> np.random.seed(1)
>>> Z = np.random.binomial(1, 0.5, 100).reshape(-1, 1)
>>> x = Weibull.random(100, 10, 2) * np.exp(-0.5 * Z[:, 0])
>>> model = WeibullPH.fit(x, Z)
>>> round(float(model.at([0]).mean()), 3)
8.575
bic() → float

The Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) for the model, if it was fit with the fit() method. Not available if fit with the from_params() method.

Returns:

bic – The BIC of the model

Return type:

float

Examples

>>> from surpyval import Weibull
>>> import numpy as np
>>> np.random.seed(1)
>>> x = Weibull.random(100, 10, 3)
>>> model = Weibull.fit(x)
>>> model.bic()
np.float64(534.2640532197888)

References

Bayesian Information Criterion for Censored Survival Models.

Notes

The sample size \(d\) in the penalty \(k \ln d\) is the number of observed failures: every unit whose failure was observed, exactly or within a left- or interval-censored window, weighted by its count; right-censored units add nothing. Should that be zero, the number of units is used instead, so the criterion is always finite. Every model in SurPyval that reports a BIC counts \(d\) this way (see “Information criteria” in the Parametric Estimation guide).

cb(x: npt.ArrayLike, Z: npt.ArrayLike | pd.DataFrame, on: str = 'sf', alpha_ci: float = 0.05, bound: str = 'two-sided', method: str = 'wald', n_boot: int = 200, random_state: Any = None, robust: bool = False, cluster: npt.ArrayLike | None = None) → npt.NDArray

Confidence bounds on a predicted function at covariate vector Z.

With method="wald" (the default) the bounds propagate the fitted parameter covariance through the requested function by the delta method. sf/ff/Hf are derived from one bound on the baseline family’s probability-plot scale, as for the univariate models: log H for a Weibull, Exponential, Rayleigh or Gumbel baseline, the normal quantile of F for a Normal or LogNormal one, the logit of F for the rest (#504; every band was on the logit before v0.22). Each keeps sf in (0, 1), and is formed from the cumulative hazard so the Hf bound has no ceiling where sf underflows. hf/df use a log-scale bound (so they stay positive).

method="lr" gives the likelihood-ratio bound instead, as for the univariate models’ cb(method="lr"): at each x and row of Z the bound is the extreme of the function over the likelihood region of all the parameters, {theta : 2[nll(theta) - nll_hat] <= chi2_1}, which is where the function’s profile deviance reaches the critical value; the sf, ff and Hf bounds are one bound, so they agree exactly. It does not rest on the function being near linear in the parameters, and is invariant to their parameterisation, but takes a search of the likelihood: about a second a bound, where the Wald bound takes milliseconds (the region’s boundary is traced once per model and level, and kept). It needs the data the model was fitted to; where a bound cannot be found it is nan, with a warning. Both are large-sample bounds, and neither is exact with few failures: on an accelerated life test of 72 units extrapolated 40 °C below its coolest cell (#583), the 90% bounds on the five-year reliability at the use condition covered 0.897 (Wald) and 0.893 (likelihood ratio) with 46 failures on average (1000 repetitions), and 0.877 and 0.866 with 11 (900).

method="bootstrap" gives a parametric bootstrap bound: the model is refitted to n_boot data sets simulated from it, each unit at its own covariates and within its own truncation window, and censored as it was – a censored unit at its censoring time, a failed one at a time drawn from the censoring distribution past its failure (Davison & Hinkley’s conditional bootstrap), so a test stopped at a common time censors every unit there. The bound is the BCa interval of the refits’ values (Efron 1987: their percentiles, corrected for bias and for skewness, the acceleration taken from each resample’s score at the estimate); sf, ff and Hf are one interval. On the test above with 46 failures it covered 0.903, against 0.880 (Wald), 0.875 (likelihood ratio) and 0.866 for the plain percentile interval (1000 repetitions of 1000 refits, #617). With 11 failures it covered 0.71 (Wald 0.87, likelihood ratio 0.85): in 28% of those data sets the likelihood has no finite maximum, and a bootstrap from such a fit closes onto its estimate (it warns so); where the estimate exists it covered 0.979. A refit that reaches no verified maximum (a resample with no failures at some stresses can leave an effect without one) is kept at the estimate it reached, and one that raises is left out; both are counted, with one warning when more than 2% of the refits are. It needs the data, and is not available for left- or interval-censored data or a time-varying-covariate fit. It costs n_boot refits: about 60 s for 1000 on that test with WeibullAFT. With an integer random_state the refits are kept, and shared by every bound with the same n_boot and seed.

Parameters:

  • x (array like or scalar) – Times at which to evaluate the bound(s).

  • Z (array like) – A single covariate vector, used at every x (one row per x is paired element-wise, as for sf()).

  • on ({'sf', 'ff', 'Hf', 'hf', 'df'}, optional) – The function to bound. Default 'sf'.

  • alpha_ci (float, optional) – Total tail probability of the bound(s). Default 0.05.

  • bound ({'two-sided', 'lower', 'upper'}, optional) – Two-sided bounds put [lower, upper] on the last axis.

  • method ({'wald', 'lr', 'bootstrap'}, optional) – 'wald' (the default), 'lr' or 'bootstrap', as above ('lr' also as 'likelihood', 'likelihood-ratio' or 'profile').

  • n_boot (int, optional) – The number of bootstrap refits (method='bootstrap' only). Default 200; a bound at a 5% tail is steadier with 1000 or more.

  • random_state (None, int or numpy.random.Generator, optional) – The seed of the bootstrap (method='bootstrap' only). None (the default) draws from numpy’s global generator, so np.random.seed reproduces it; an int or a Generator gives a stream of its own. With an int the refits are kept on the model, and every cb, param_cb, quantile_cb and cb_tvc with the same n_boot and seed reuses them.

  • robust (bool, optional) – True propagates the robust (sandwich) covariance, robust_covariance(), instead of the model-based one, as summary(robust=True) does; method must be "wald". Default False.

  • cluster (array_like, optional) – With robust=True, a cluster label for each row given to the fit (as for robust_covariance()).

Returns:

The confidence bound(s) on on at each x.

Return type:

numpy array

cb_tvc(x: ArrayLike, Z: ArrayLike | Any, xl: ArrayLike | None = None, given: float | None = None, on: str = 'sf', alpha_ci: float = 0.05, bound: str = 'two-sided', method: str = 'wald', n_boot: int = 200, random_state: Any = None) → NDArray

Confidence bounds on the survival, failure probability or cumulative hazard along a covariate path Z(t): a step schedule or a continuously varying path, as for sf_tvc().

The bounds are those of cb(), carried along the path. With method="wald" (the default), a Wald bound on the baseline family’s probability-plot scale, formed from the cumulative hazard of Hf_tvc(), its standard error propagated from the fitted parameter covariance by the delta method. With method="lr", the likelihood-ratio bound of cb(): at each x the extreme of the function along the path over the likelihood region of all the parameters (#617), about a second a time where the Wald bound takes milliseconds; it needs the data the model was fitted to. With method="bootstrap", the BCa interval (as for cb()) over the parametric bootstrap refits of cb() (with the same n_boot and integer random_state it reuses them); not for a model fitted to time-varying covariates, whose resamples would need each subject’s covariate path. Either way ff and Hf follow from the same bound, so the three agree with each other, and a constant path gives cb() with the same method.

Along a CovariatePath the integral is taken on a quadrature mesh adapted at the fitted parameters and then held fixed, so the function differentiated (or searched) is smooth in the parameters. The Wald bound’s cost is 2k + 1 evaluations along the path for k parameters.

With given the bounds are on the conditional survival \(S(x \mid \text{survived to } g)\) of sf_tvc(): 1, with no width, at and before given.

Parameters:

  • x (array_like) – Times at which to bound the function.

  • Z (StepSchedule, CovariatePath or array_like) – The covariate path, as for sf_tvc().

  • xl (array_like, optional) – Segment start times, required only when Z is an array.

  • given (float, optional) – Condition on survival to this age, as for sf_tvc(). A nan given gives nan.

  • on ({'sf', 'ff', 'Hf'}, optional) – The function to bound ('R' and 'F' are accepted for 'sf' and 'ff'). Default 'sf'. The hazard and the density along a path are not bounded.

  • alpha_ci (float, optional) – Total tail probability of the bound(s). Default 0.05.

  • bound ({'two-sided', 'lower', 'upper'}, optional) – Two-sided bounds put [lower, upper] on the last axis.

  • method ({'wald', 'lr', 'bootstrap'}, optional) – 'wald' (the default), 'lr' or 'bootstrap', as above and as for cb() ('lr' also as 'likelihood', 'likelihood-ratio' or 'profile').

  • n_boot (int, optional) – The number of bootstrap refits (method='bootstrap' only). Default 200.

  • random_state (None, int or numpy.random.Generator, optional) – The seed of the bootstrap (method='bootstrap' only), as for cb().

Returns:

The confidence bound(s) on on at each x: the query’s shape, with [lower, upper] on a last axis for two-sided bounds.

Return type:

numpy array

Examples

A proportional hazards model along a stress ramped from 0 to 1 over 50 hours:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from surpyval import CovariatePath, WeibullPH
>>> rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
>>> Z = rng.uniform(0, 1, (200, 1))
>>> x = 100 * rng.weibull(2, 200) * np.exp(-0.5 * Z[:, 0])
>>> model = WeibullPH.fit(x, Z)
>>> ramp = CovariatePath.from_points([0, 50], [0.0, 1.0])
>>> model.sf_tvc([40, 80], ramp).round(4)
array([0.771 , 0.1911])
>>> model.cb_tvc([40, 80], ramp).round(4)
array([[0.7243, 0.8109],
       [0.1256, 0.267 ]])

A constant path gives the ordinary bounds:

>>> flat = CovariatePath.from_points([0], [0.5])
>>> bool(np.allclose(model.cb_tvc([40, 80], flat),
...                  model.cb(np.array([40, 80]), [0.5])))
True
center: npt.NDArray | None = None

zeros (or None, for an accelerated life model) when they are those of a unit with Z = 0, the default. A fit with center=True keeps its baseline at the n-weighted covariate means (#463), stored here, and every prediction uses Z - center.

Type:

The covariate point the baseline parameters are at

common_shape_test() → dict

The likelihood-ratio test that the distribution’s shape is the same at every stress level, as an accelerated life model assumes.

At each distinct stress (each distinct row of Z) the baseline distribution is fitted on its own, its life and shape free; and all levels together with one shape and a life of their own each. Twice the difference of the maximised log-likelihoods is, under a common shape, \(\chi^2\) with k - 1 degrees of freedom for k levels (Nelson, Accelerated Testing, 1990, ch. 9; Meeker and Escobar, 1998, section 19.4). Neither likelihood involves the life-stress relation, so the test is of the shape alone.

A level with fewer than two failures has no shape of its own: it is left out of the test, with a warning naming it and its failures.

Returns:

"statistic", "df", "p_value", "shapes" (each level’s own, by its stress), "common_shape", "levels" (the stresses tested, as tuples), "log_likelihood_separate", "log_likelihood_common", "parameter" (the shape’s name) and "left_out" (the levels left out, with their failures).

Return type:

dict

Raises:

ValueError – If the model is not an accelerated life model, has no data or was fitted with weights, its distribution has not exactly one parameter beside the life, or fewer than two levels have two failures.

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import surpyval as sp
>>> from surpyval import life_models
>>> rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
>>> T = np.repeat([358.15, 378.15, 398.15], 20)
>>> life = 1e-6 * np.exp(0.7 / 8.617333262e-5 / T)
>>> x = life * rng.weibull(2.0, T.size)
>>> model = sp.AcceleratedLife(sp.Weibull, life_models.Arrhenius)
>>> test = model.fit(x, Z=T).common_shape_test()
>>> test["df"], round(test["statistic"], 3), round(test["p_value"], 3)
(2, 0.333, 0.847)
concordance(x: ArrayLike | None = None, c: ArrayLike | None = None, Z: Any = None, tie_tol: float = 1e-08, ties: str = 'therneau', *, weighting: str = 'harrell', tau: float | None = None, alpha_ci: float = 0.05, ci_method: str = 'normal') → ConcordanceResult | float

Harrell’s (or Uno’s) concordance index (C) of the model’s risk scores, with its standard error and confidence interval.

The proportion of usable pairs of subjects – the one with the earlier time had the event – in which the model gives that subject the higher risk: 1 ranks every pair correctly, 0.5 is chance. With no arguments it scores the data the model was fitted to (each row counted n times); pass x, c and Z together to score other data, such as a test set. Two events at the same time are not a pair (ties="therneau", as R’s concordance and lifelines) unless ties="harrell"; see surpyval.metrics.concordance_index() for the treatment of tied times and scores.

The risk score, higher meaning an earlier event, is for each family:

  • CoxPH, the frailty models and AdditiveHazards (Lin-Ying): the linear predictor \(\beta'Z\) (the log hazard ratio, or the covariates’ additive hazard), as R’s concordance and lifelines use;

  • the parametric families (PH, AFT, PO, AH and the accelerated life models): the cumulative hazard \(H(t^* \mid Z)\) at \(t^*\), the median of the times scored. For every family whose covariates act through a linear predictor this ranks the rows exactly as the linear predictor does, with the sign that means a higher risk (\(\beta'Z\) for PH, AFT and AH, \(-\beta'Z\) for PO), and \(t^*\) does not matter; it can only matter for an accelerated life model whose life model sets a shape parameter;

  • BuckleyJames: \(-\beta'Z\), since the model is linear in the log time;

  • ProportionalOdds: \(-\beta'Z\), the log of the odds of failure relative to the baseline’s.

Parameters:

  • x (array_like, optional) – Observed times.

  • c (array_like, optional) – Censoring flags, 0 an event and 1 right censored.

  • Z (array_like or DataFrame, optional) – Covariates, one row per time (a DataFrame for a model fitted with fit_from_df).

  • tie_tol (float, optional) – Scores within this of each other are tied. Default 1e-8.

  • ties ({"therneau", "harrell"}, optional) – "therneau" (the default, as R’s survival::concordance and lifelines): two events at the same time are not a usable pair. "harrell" (Harrell’s original definition): they are, counting 1 if their scores are tied, else 0.5.

  • weighting ({"harrell", "uno"}, optional) – "harrell" (default): every usable pair weighs 1. "uno": Uno’s inverse-probability-of-censoring weighted C, each pair weighted by 1 / G(t-)^2 (see surpyval.metrics.concordance_index()).

  • tau (float, optional) – Count only the pairs whose earlier time is at most tau. Default None, every pair.

  • alpha_ci (float, optional) – Keyword only: the significance level of the interval. Default 0.05.

  • ci_method ({"normal", "logit"}, optional) – Keyword only: the scale of the interval. Default "normal".

Returns:

The concordance index, a float that carries its infinitesimal-jackknife standard error se and interval ci (surpyval.metrics.concordance_index()). With no data it scores the data the model was fitted to, each row repeated n times as its own subject (as R does with the rows repeated); the standard error treats the scores as fixed, as R’s does. A plain nan where a covariate is missing.

Return type:

ConcordanceResult

Raises:

ValueError – If only some of x, c and Z are given, or none are and the model does not keep its training data (a model restored with from_dict, or one fitted with time-varying covariates, whose rows are intervals of a subject’s history).

Examples

>>> import surpyval as sp
>>> from surpyval.datasets import load_lung
>>> lung = load_lung().dropna(subset=["ph.ecog"])
>>> lung["censored"] = 1 - lung["status"]  # status 1 is a death
>>> model = sp.CoxPH.fit_from_df(
...     lung, x_col="time", c_col="censored",
...     Z_cols=["age", "sex", "ph.ecog"],
... )
>>> round(model.concordance(), 4)
0.6371
>>> round(model.concordance(ties="harrell"), 4)
0.6369
concordance_estimate(x: ArrayLike | None = None, c: ArrayLike | None = None, Z: Any = None, *, weighting: str = 'harrell', tau: float | None = None, alpha: float = 0.05, tie_tol: float = 1e-08, ties: str = 'therneau', ci_method: str = 'normal') → ConcordanceResult

Deprecated: concordance() gives the standard error and interval (alpha_ci= for alpha); this name is removed in v0.30.

The model’s concordance index with its standard error and confidence interval (R’s concordance(fit)).

The index and the scores are concordance()’s; the standard error is the infinitesimal jackknife of surpyval.metrics.concordance_index(). With no data it scores the data the model was fitted to, each row repeated n times as its own subject, and so as R does with the rows repeated, not with n as case weights. The standard error treats the scores as fixed: it does not include the uncertainty of the fitted coefficients, as R’s does not.

Parameters:

  • x (array_like, optional) – Observed times.

  • c (array_like, optional) – Censoring flags, 0 an event and 1 right censored.

  • Z (array_like or DataFrame, optional) – Covariates, one row per time.

  • weighting ({"harrell", "uno"}, optional) – Harrell’s C (default) or Uno’s IPCW C.

  • tau (float, optional) – Count only the pairs whose earlier time is at most tau.

  • alpha (float, optional) – Significance level of the interval. Default 0.05.

  • tie_tol (float, optional) – Scores within this of each other are tied. Default 1e-8.

  • ties ({"therneau", "harrell"}, optional) – How two events at the same time count. Default "therneau".

  • ci_method ({"normal", "logit"}, optional) – The scale of the interval. Default "normal".

Returns:

The estimate, se, ci and the weighted pair counts.

Return type:

ConcordanceResult

Raises:

ValueError – As concordance(); or if a covariate is missing, which leaves a subject’s score undefined.

Examples

>>> import surpyval as sp
>>> from surpyval.datasets import load_lung
>>> lung = load_lung().dropna(subset=["ph.ecog"])
